structures.name: Sphenoid bone
structures.what: Midline keystone bone of the skull base: a hollow body containing the [[s.sphenoid-sinus]], with paired lesser wings, greater wings and pterygoid processes.
structures.why: The optic nerves, ICAs, cavernous sinuses and pituitary all sit on or in its body, so its pneumatization pattern decides how safe and how wide every posterior sinus and ventral skull base approach is.

rel.note: via the clival (dorsum) part of the body

structures.ct: Axial and sagittal: the central bone behind the ethmoid; the body is the air block beneath the sella; the wings fan laterally at the orbital apex and middle fossa.

pearls.text: Body = sinus + sella turcica; lesser wings = optic canal roof and anterior clinoids; greater wings = middle fossa floor with foramina rotundum, ovale and spinosum; pterygoid processes = the posterior wall of the PPF.

The body meets the basiocciput at the spheno-occipital synchondrosis, inside the [[s.clivus]] behind the sphenoid floor; it stays open until adolescence, so on pediatric and teenage CT it is a normal lucent line, not a clival fracture.

structures.name: Sphenoid sinus
structures.what: Paired air space in the sphenoid body, the most posterior paranasal sinus, draining through its ostium into the [[s.sphenoethmoidal-recess]].
structures.why: It is the anterior door to the sella, clivus and cavernous sinuses, and its lateral wall carries the optic nerve and ICA — often under paper-thin or absent bone. Every cut inside it is decided by the CT, not by feel.

rel.note: sellar and postsellar types; in a presellar sinus the sella is posterosuperior
its floor is part of the nasopharyngeal roof
parasellar and paraclival segments bulge into its lateral and posterior walls

structures.ct: Axial: the air space behind the posterior ethmoid and in front of the clivus, with the carotid canals as round bony bulges posterolaterally. Sagittal: the sella sits on its roof. Coronal through the sella: optic canals superolateral, ICAs lateral, V2 and vidian canal inferolateral.
structures.endo: Right, 0°: through a wide sphenoidotomy the posterior wall shows the sellar bulge in the center, planum above, clival recess below, carotid prominences lateral and optic prominences superolateral.

pearls.text: Walls: roof = planum and sella; lateral = optic canal, ICA, cavernous sinus; floor = vidian canal and nasopharynx roof; posterior = clivus; anterior = the sphenoid face with the ostium.

The two sinuses are almost never symmetric; the [[s.intersinus-septum]] is midline anteriorly but deviates posteriorly, so one sinus can wrap behind the other and place its ICA on the "wrong" side of the septum.

Pneumatization ([[c.sphenoid-pneumatization]]) decides the approach: conchal and presellar sinuses need drilling of solid bone to reach the sella under navigation; postsellar and laterally extended sinuses put the ICA, optic nerve and V2 into relief and closer to the instruments.

structures.name: Sphenoid sinus ostium
syn: natural ostium of the sphenoid sinus
structures.what: The natural opening of the sphenoid sinus, high on its anterior wall, draining into the [[s.sphenoethmoidal-recess]] usually just medial to the [[s.superior-turbinate]].
structures.why: It is the safe, reproducible entry point to the sphenoid; enlarging it inferiorly and medially avoids the optic nerve and ICA that sit superolaterally in the sinus.

rel.note: the artery crosses the sphenoid face between ostium and choana

structures.ct: Sagittal or axial through the SER: a gap in the upper anterior sinus wall, medial to the posterior end of the superior turbinate, roughly 1–1.5 cm above the choanal arch ([[m.choana-to-sphenoid-ostium]]).
structures.endo: Either side, 0°: slide between septum and middle turbinate to the SER; the slit-like ostium sits medial to the superior turbinate at about the level of its inferior third. If hidden, gently lateralize or trim the inferior third of the superior turbinate.

pearls.text: Being high on the anterior wall, the ostium is not dependent: drainage relies on mucociliary clearance, which is why a sphenoidotomy is enlarged inferiorly.
A small posterior ethmoid cell opening in the superior meatus can mimic it; the true ostium is medial to the superior turbinate, a meatal opening is lateral to it.

It often lies at about the height of the maxillary sinus roof: after an antrostomy, the orbital floor seen through it gives a working height for sphenoid entry, and staying at or below that plane keeps you under the skull base.

structures.name: Sphenoethmoidal recess
structures.what: Narrow slot of the posterosuperior nasal cavity between the [[s.nasal-septum]] and the [[s.superior-turbinate]], in front of the sphenoid face, into which the sphenoid ostium opens.
structures.why: It is where you find the sphenoid ostium transnasally without opening the ethmoid, and where posterior-group disease (sphenoid and posterior ethmoid) drains toward the nasopharynx.

rel.note: passing posterosuperior to the torus tubarius

structures.ct: Axial at the level of the superior turbinate: the air slot between septum and superior turbinate directly in front of the sphenoid face.
structures.endo: Either side, 0°: advance medial to the middle turbinate along the septum above the choana; the SER opens medial to the superior turbinate.

structures.name: Anterior wall of the sphenoid sinus
structures.what: The anterior bony wall of each sphenoid sinus, facing the SER medially and the last posterior ethmoid cell laterally; it carries the ostium and, in the midline, the rostrum.
structures.why: You open it to make a sphenoidotomy. Its inferior part is crossed by the posterior septal artery (the nasoseptal flap pedicle), so taking the face down to the floor costs that artery unless the flap is raised first.

rel.note: its lateral part, via the transethmoidal route

structures.endo: Either side, 0°: the flat bone behind the superior turbinate; transethmoidally, the posteroinferior wall of the last posterior ethmoid cell, medial and inferior to it.

structures.name: Sphenoid rostrum
structures.what: Midline keel on the inferior sphenoid face, clasped by the alae of the vomer, from which the intersinus septum rises posteriorly.
structures.why: It is the most reliable midline marker at the posterior nasal cavity — more reliable than the intersinus septum — and is drilled flat to join the two sphenoidotomies into one working cavity.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: after a posterior septectomy, the thick midline wedge between the two sphenoid ostia, below them.

structures.name: Intersinus septum of the sphenoid
structures.what: Bony partition between the right and left sphenoid sinuses; midline anteriorly at the rostrum but often deviated and oblique posteriorly.
structures.why: Its posterior insertion can be on the carotid prominence or optic canal ([[v.intersinus-septum-on-ica]]), so twisting it off can fracture the canal and tear the ICA. Remove it with a drill or through-cutting instrument after reading its insertion on axial CT.

rel.note: posterior end, in a substantial subset; see [[v.intersinus-septum-on-ica]]

structures.ct: Axial through the sphenoid: follow the septum from the rostrum back to where it meets the posterior or lateral wall and note whether that point is the carotid canal or optic canal. Repeat for every accessory septum.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: the vertical plate dividing the two sinuses after bilateral sphenoidotomy; do not assume it marks the midline of the sella.

pearls.text: Never twist or rock a septum off the back wall; cut it or drill it down.
Use the rostrum/vomer and the sellar bulge, not the septum, to define the midline.

structures.name: Accessory sphenoid septum
structures.what: Additional sagittal, oblique or horizontal bony plates within a sphenoid sinus, separate from the main intersinus septum.
structures.why: Accessory septa commonly run to the carotid prominence or optic canal and can split the sinus into compartments that mimic a small sinus or a false sellar floor; each is traced on CT and removed like the main septum.
structures.ct: Axial and coronal: any bony plate other than the main septum; note its insertion as for the main septum.

structures.name: Floor of the sphenoid sinus
structures.what: The inferior wall of the sphenoid sinus, forming part of the nasopharyngeal roof; the vidian canal runs at its junction with the lateral wall.
structures.why: It marks the boundary between the middle and lower clivus in the endonasal model, and the vidian canal in its lateral edge is the guide to the petrous ICA.
structures.ct: Coronal through the pterygoid base: the vidian canal is the small round canal in the floor-lateral wall angle, inferomedial to the foramen rotundum.

structures.name: Lateral wall of the sphenoid sinus
structures.what: The thin lateral bony wall of the sphenoid sinus separating it from the cavernous sinus, ICA and optic canal.
structures.why: This is the dangerous wall. From top to bottom it shows the optic prominence, the lateral opticocarotid recess, the carotid prominence and (if pneumatized laterally) the V2 bulge; the bone may be dehiscent over any of them.
structures.ct: Coronal through the sella: identify, from superior to inferior, optic canal, ICA, then V2 in foramen rotundum; check each for bony dehiscence.
structures.endo: Right, 0°: the posterolateral wall of the right sphenoid; the optic prominence runs obliquely toward the planum above, the carotid prominence curves vertically below it.

pearls.text: No instrument pushes against the lateral wall. Suction and mucosal work here are done gently and under direct view.

structures.name: Lateral recess of the sphenoid sinus
syn: lateral extension of the sphenoid sinus
structures.what: Extension of the sphenoid air space lateral to a line between the vidian canal and foramen rotundum, into the pterygoid base and greater wing.
structures.why: It is a classic site of spontaneous CSF leak and meningoencephalocele (thin middle fossa floor) and is out of reach of a straight transnasal sphenoidotomy — it needs angled scopes from the opposite nostril or a transpterygoid corridor.

rel.note: V2 bulges into its superolateral wall

structures.ct: Coronal through the pterygoid base: air extending lateral to the vidian canal, under and around the foramen rotundum.
structures.endo: Left recess, 45°: from the right nostril across a posterior septectomy, rotated laterally; V2 is the ridge in the roof-lateral wall.

pearls.text: Leak in a lateral recess: plan a transpterygoid approach (or at least a contralateral angled view) rather than blind packing.

Lateral recess leaks are usually attributed to a thin, extensively pneumatized middle fossa floor with arachnoid pits under raised CSF pressure; a persistent lateral craniopharyngeal (Sternberg) canal is a debated alternative explanation. Treat raised intracranial pressure as part of the repair.

structures.name: Clival recess of the sphenoid sinus
structures.what: Part of the sphenoid sinus below the sella, where pneumatization extends posteriorly into the sphenoidal clivus (the middle third in the endonasal scheme) between the paraclival carotid prominences.
structures.why: Its posterior wall is the middle clivus: the window for transclival approaches, bounded laterally by the paraclival ICAs.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: the concavity under the sellar bulge; the paraclival carotid prominences form its lateral margins.

structures.name: Carotid prominence
structures.what: Bony bulge of the ICA into the lateral and posterior walls of the sphenoid sinus: a vertical paraclival part below the sella and a parasellar part lateral to it, turning under the optic prominence at the paraclinoid segment.
structures.why: It shows you where the ICA is — and the bone over it can be under 1 mm or absent ([[v.ica-dehiscence]]). Nothing is pushed, twisted or coagulated with monopolar on it.

rel.note: lateral limit of the sellar opening

structures.ct: Axial below the sella: round bulges at the posterolateral sinus corners (paraclival). Coronal through the sella: the ICA lateral to the sellar floor. Check bony covering on bone windows.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°, after wide sphenoidotomy: two vertical ridges framing the clival recess and sella, continuous superiorly with the lOCR under the optic prominence.

pearls.text: Optic above, carotid below, lOCR between — on each side of the sphenoid posterior wall.
In a poorly pneumatized (conchal or presellar) sinus there may be no visible prominence at all; navigation and Doppler replace the missing landmark.
Labib's endoscopic segments map onto the prominence: paraclival (vertical, beside the clival recess), parasellar (beside the sella), paraclinoid (under the lOCR); see [[c.ica-endoscopic-segments]].

structures.name: Optic prominence
structures.what: Bony ridge of the optic canal in the superolateral wall of the sphenoid sinus (and sometimes of the last posterior ethmoid cell), running from the orbital apex back toward the tuberculum.
structures.why: It marks the optic nerve, which may be covered by very thin or dehiscent bone ([[v.optic-canal-dehiscence]]). It is the superior lateral limit of any sphenoid work and the target of optic nerve decompression.
structures.ct: Coronal through the posterior sphenoid: the optic canal as a round canal at the superolateral corner; axial: the canal running anterolaterally toward the orbital apex.
structures.endo: Right, 0°: an oblique ridge at the top of the lateral wall converging medially toward the tuberculum; the lOCR lies directly beneath it laterally.

structures.name: Lateral opticocarotid recess
structures.what: Depression in the lateral sphenoid wall between the optic prominence above and the carotid prominence below, formed by pneumatization of the optic strut.
structures.why: It is the single best endoscopic landmark in the sphenoid: it pins the optic nerve (above), the paraclinoid ICA (below and behind) and the anterior clinoid (laterally). Drilling it removes the optic strut to decompress the optic canal from below.

rel.note: it is the pneumatized optic strut seen from the sinus

structures.ct: Coronal through the anterior clinoid: the air pocket between the optic canal (superomedial) and the ICA (inferolateral); if the anterior clinoid is pneumatized the recess continues into it ([[v.pneumatized-anterior-clinoid]]).
structures.endo: Right, 0°: a teardrop-shaped dimple at the superolateral corner of the sinus, pointing laterally, between the oblique optic ridge and the curving carotid ridge.

pearls.text: Find the lOCR on both sides first; the sella is centered between them at a lower level, and the planum lies between the optic prominences above.
Behind the lOCR is the clinoid (C5) ICA between proximal and distal dural rings; drilling the strut exposes both the optic sheath and the carotid collar.

structures.name: Medial opticocarotid recess
structures.what: Small notch at the lateral end of the tuberculum sellae where the medial end of the optic canal meets the paraclinoid carotid prominence; it corresponds intracranially to the lateral tubercular crest / middle clinoid.
structures.why: It marks the medial limit of the paraclinoid ICA and the entry of the optic nerve into its canal, so it defines the lateral edge of transtuberculum bone removal and the point where you open the medial optic canal.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: at the upper lateral corner of the sellar bulge, where the tuberculum meets the paraclinoid carotid; less obvious than the lOCR and often only seen after the mucosa is removed.

pearls.text: Drilling the mOCR opens the medial optic canal and exposes the medial distal dural ring; the superior hypophyseal artery arises just above it on the supraclinoid ICA.

structures.name: Greater wing of the sphenoid
structures.what: Lateral wing of the sphenoid forming the anterior middle fossa floor and part of the lateral orbital wall; it carries the foramina rotundum, ovale and spinosum.
structures.why: Lateral recess pneumatization into it brings V2 and middle fossa dura into the sinus, which is where spontaneous lateral recess leaks arise.

rel.note: the superior orbital fissure lies between them

structures.name: Lesser wing of the sphenoid
structures.what: Thin upper wing forming the posterior anterior-fossa floor; its two roots enclose the optic canal and it ends medially as the anterior clinoid process.
structures.why: Its inferior root is the optic strut (the lOCR from below), so it is the bone you drill to decompress the optic canal and to reach the clinoid ICA.

rel.note: roof and, via the optic strut, floor

structures.name: Optic canal
structures.what: Bony canal between the roots of the lesser wing and the sphenoid body, transmitting the [[s.optic-nerve]] and [[s.ophthalmic-artery]] from the middle cranial fossa to the orbital apex.
structures.why: Its medial wall is the thinnest point between the sinus and the optic nerve; it is the site of traumatic optic neuropathy, of compressive lesions, and of endoscopic decompression.

rel.note: coronal CT through the sphenoid: optic canal at the top of the lateral wall, foramen rotundum (V2) below it, vidian canal at the floor

structures.ct: Axial: runs anterolaterally from the chiasmatic sulcus to the orbital apex, lateral to the sphenoid or an Onodi cell. Coronal: round canal superomedial to the anterior clinoid, above the lOCR.
structures.endo: Right, 0°: the optic prominence in the superolateral sphenoid wall or in the lateral wall of an Onodi cell.

pearls.text: If a sphenoethmoidal (Onodi) cell is present the canal runs in its lateral wall, not the sphenoid's — the "sphenoid" you are in may be that cell.

Inside the canal the nerve sheath is fused to the periosteum, so the nerve cannot move away from swelling or bone fragments; that is why intracanalicular injury is poorly tolerated and why decompression extends forward to the annulus of Zinn.

Through the canal the dura is in two layers: an outer layer that continues into the orbit as the periorbita, and an inner layer that becomes the nerve's own sheath, tethered to the arachnoid. They part at the orbital opening, where the annulus of Zinn surrounds the nerve.

structures.name: Optic strut
syn: inferior root of the lesser wing
structures.what: Bony bar from the lesser wing to the sphenoid body forming the floor of the optic canal and separating it from the superior orbital fissure.
structures.why: Endoscopically it is the lOCR; the clinoid ICA lies against its posterior surface, so drilling it decompresses the optic canal from below but brings the bur onto the carotid.

structures.name: Anterior clinoid process
structures.what: Posteromedial projection of the lesser wing, lateral to the optic canal, overhanging the ICA as it leaves the cavernous sinus.
structures.why: Its inferior surface bears the proximal dural ring and its upper surface the distal ring; the clinoid ICA lies between. Pneumatization makes it part of the sinus ([[v.pneumatized-anterior-clinoid]]) and brings that ICA segment into the drilling field.

rel.note: CN III runs under its tip in the cavernous roof

structures.ct: Coronal and axial at the orbital apex: triangular bone lateral to the optic canal; air within it = pneumatized clinoid.

structures.name: Middle clinoid process
structures.what: Inconstant small spur at the lateral end of the tuberculum sellae, medial to the clinoid ICA; it may bridge to the anterior clinoid ([[v.caroticoclinoid-foramen]]).
structures.why: It sits behind the medial opticocarotid recess; an ossified caroticoclinoid ring around the ICA here makes bone removal at the mOCR riskier.

structures.name: Superior orbital fissure
structures.what: Cleft between the greater and lesser sphenoid wings, inferolateral to the optic canal, connecting the cavernous sinus to the orbit.
structures.why: It carries CN III, IV, V1 and VI and the superior ophthalmic vein; cavernous sinus lesions and orbital apex surgery affect them together (orbital apex / SOF syndrome).

structures.name: Planum sphenoidale
structures.what: Flat roof of the sphenoid sinus between the optic canals, continuous anteriorly with the cribriform plate and ending posteriorly at the limbus.
structures.why: It is the skull base immediately in front of the chiasm: the roof you follow during sphenoidotomy and the bone removed in transplanum approaches to suprasellar tumors.
structures.ct: Sagittal: the flat roof line of the sphenoid from the posterior ethmoid roof to the tuberculum; coronal: the roof between the two optic canals.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: the smooth roof of the sinus above the sellar bulge; followed anteriorly it continues level with, or rises slightly into, the posterior ethmoid roof at the level of the posterior ethmoidal artery.

pearls.text: Once the sphenoid roof is identified, follow the skull base from behind forward during ethmoidectomy — the planum is a safe, flat reference height.
Transplanum bone removal is bounded by the optic canals laterally, the posterior ethmoidal arteries anteriorly (to spare olfaction) and the tuberculum posteriorly.

structures.name: Limbus sphenoidale
structures.what: Transverse ridge at the posterior edge of the planum, marking the front of the chiasmatic sulcus.
structures.why: It is the anterior edge of the prechiasmatic space and the usual anterior limit of dural opening in a transtuberculum approach.

structures.name: Chiasmatic sulcus
structures.what: Shallow transverse groove between the limbus and the tuberculum sellae, leading laterally into the optic canals.
structures.why: Its length and angle determine how much room lies in front of the chiasm; a short sulcus with a prefixed chiasm leaves little prechiasmatic working space.

structures.name: Tuberculum sellae
structures.what: Bony prominence forming the anterior-superior lip of the sella turcica, between the chiasmatic sulcus and the hypophyseal fossa.
structures.why: Endonasally it is the angle between planum and sellar face; the superior intercavernous sinus lies just below it, and removing it opens the prechiasmatic space for suprasellar tumors.
structures.ct: Sagittal: the angle where the planum turns down into the anterior sellar wall.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: the transverse bony bar at the top of the sellar bulge, between the two mOCRs; the "sellar–tubercular angle".

structures.name: Sella turcica
structures.what: Saddle-shaped depression on the upper sphenoid body that holds the pituitary gland; endonasally its floor bulges into the roof and posterior wall of the sphenoid sinus.
structures.why: Its floor is the door for transsphenoidal surgery. On the sinus side it is centered between the carotid prominences, below the tuberculum and above the clival recess.
structures.ct: Sagittal: the cup on top of the sphenoid body between tuberculum and dorsum; size in [[m.sella-ap-diameter]] and [[m.sella-depth]]. Coronal: flanked by the cavernous ICAs.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: the smooth rounded bulge in the center of the posterior sphenoid wall; lighter and bluish if the bone is thinned by an adenoma.

pearls.text: Sella center, carotids on either side, optic nerves above and lateral, planum above, clival recess below: the "face" of the sphenoid.

Macroadenomas expand and thin the floor and push the carotids apart; small microadenomas and Cushing disease leave a normal-sized sella, so the opening must still be wide enough to explore both halves of the gland.

structures.name: Dorsum sellae
structures.what: Square plate of bone forming the posterior wall of the sella and the top of the clivus, crowned laterally by the posterior clinoid processes.
structures.why: It is the upper third of the clivus in the endonasal model; removing it (after pituitary transposition) opens the interpeduncular cistern and basilar apex.

rel.note: the basilar apex lies behind and above it

structures.ct: Sagittal: the upright posterior sellar wall; axial through the sella: the transverse bar behind the gland.

structures.name: Posterior clinoid process
structures.what: Tubercle at each upper lateral corner of the dorsum sellae, giving attachment to the interclinoid and petroclinoid dural folds.
structures.why: It is removed in endonasal posterior clinoidectomy to reach retrosellar and interpeduncular lesions; CN III passes just lateral to it into the cavernous roof.

structures.name: Sellar dura
syn: dura of the anterior sellar wall
structures.what: Two-layered dura lining the sella: an outer periosteal (endosteal) layer and an inner meningeal layer, which laterally becomes the medial wall of the cavernous sinus.
structures.why: The intercavernous sinuses run between its two layers, so the site and shape of the dural opening decide how much venous bleeding you meet; the interdural plane is used for pituitary transposition.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: gray-white, sometimes bluish where an intercavernous sinus shows through, once the sellar bone is removed.

structures.name: Anterior intercavernous sinus
structures.what: Venous channel between the dural layers along the upper anterior sellar wall, just below the tuberculum, connecting the two cavernous sinuses.
structures.why: Opening the dura through it causes brisk venous bleeding; place the sellar dural incision below it, or coagulate and divide it deliberately when a transtuberculum exposure is needed.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: a transverse blue band in the upper sellar dura; it may cover the whole anterior wall ([[v.large-anterior-intercavernous-sinus]]).

structures.name: Posterior intercavernous sinus
structures.what: Venous channel behind the gland along the dorsum sellae, connecting the cavernous sinuses and continuous below with the basilar plexus.
structures.why: It bleeds during pituitary transposition and posterior clinoidectomy; control with hemostatic matrix and gentle pressure rather than cautery near the cavernous ICA.

structures.name: Diaphragma sellae
structures.what: Dural roof of the sella stretched between the tuberculum and dorsum, with a central opening for the pituitary stalk.
structures.why: It separates the sella from the CSF of the suprasellar cistern. As a macroadenoma is removed it descends into the field; a tear or a wide opening means an intraoperative CSF leak that changes the reconstruction.
structures.endo: Midline, 30° looking up: after debulking, a thin gray-white membrane billowing down with each pulse; pale arachnoid behind it signals imminent leak.

pearls.text: Remove tumor inferiorly and laterally before superiorly so the diaphragm descends last and does not hide the lateral recesses.
A wide diaphragmatic opening lets arachnoid prolapse into the sella, predisposing to leak and to an empty sella; grade any leak ([[c.csf-leak-grade]]) before choosing the repair.

structures.name: Pituitary gland
structures.what: Endocrine gland in the sella turcica: anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and posterior lobe (neurohypophysis), connected to the hypothalamus by the stalk.
structures.why: Adenomas arising from it are the commonest reason to open the sella; preserving the normal gland, which is often compressed into a thin rim, is what separates a good from a bad endocrine outcome.

rel.note: via hypophyseal veins and the intercavernous sinuses

structures.ct: CT shows only the fossa; MRI shows the gland: height in [[m.pituitary-height]], posterior lobe T1 bright spot, adenoma as a hypoenhancing focus on dynamic contrast.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°, after dural opening: normal gland is firmer and orange-tan with fine vessels; adenoma is softer, grayer and suctions easily.

pearls.text: The gland is the thing you are trying not to remove; the tumor is the thing you are.
In macroadenomas the compressed normal gland is most often pushed superiorly, posteriorly or to one side as a thin enhancing rim; find it on contrast MRI before opening the dura.

structures.name: Anterior pituitary lobe
structures.what: Glandular anterior part of the pituitary (pars distalis, intermedia, tuberalis) producing GH, PRL, ACTH, TSH, LH and FSH.
structures.why: Almost all adenomas arise here; injury or excessive resection causes anterior hypopituitarism, so tissue that looks like normal gland is preserved.

structures.name: Posterior pituitary lobe
structures.what: Neural posterior part of the pituitary, continuous with the stalk, storing and releasing ADH and oxytocin; it is the T1 bright spot on MRI.
structures.why: Handling it or the stalk causes diabetes insipidus; it is softer and more adherent to the dorsum than anterior gland.

structures.name: Pituitary stalk
structures.what: Stalk from the median eminence of the hypothalamus down through the diaphragma opening to the gland, carrying hypothalamic axons and portal vessels.
structures.why: It divides suprasellar space into pre- and retroinfundibular corridors and is the key structure to preserve in craniopharyngioma and suprasellar adenoma surgery (DI, hypopituitarism).
structures.endo: Midline, 0° or 30° through a transtuberculum opening: a pinkish-orange column with a characteristic longitudinal (portal) vascular pattern, running obliquely down and forward behind the chiasm.

pearls.text: The superior hypophyseal arteries reach the stalk from both sides; the stalk's striated portal vessels distinguish it from tumor capsule.

structures.name: Inferior hypophyseal artery
structures.what: Branch of the meningohypophyseal trunk (cavernous ICA) that runs medially to the posterior lobe and sellar floor dura.
structures.why: It is the arterial tether cut when the gland is transposed off the dorsum; tearing it at its origin bleeds from the cavernous ICA.

structures.name: Cavernous sinus
structures.what: Dural venous compartment on each side of the sella, from the superior orbital fissure to the petrous apex, containing the cavernous ICA and CN VI, with CN III, IV and V1 in its lateral wall.
structures.why: Adenomas invade it and cavernous bleeding floods the field; working in it means working around the ICA and four cranial nerves (III, IV, V1, VI), so entry is deliberate and compartment-based.
structures.ct: Contrast MRI is the imaging test: enhancing parasellar compartment around the flow-void of the ICA.
structures.endo: Right, 0°/30°: behind the parasellar carotid prominence and lateral to the sella; once the medial wall is opened, venous bleeding wells up around the ICA.

pearls.text: CN VI is the only nerve inside the sinus proper (next to the ICA); III, IV and V1 lie in its lateral wall.

Texts disagree on V2. Many list it in the lower lateral wall (five nerves); microsurgical anatomy places it below the sinus in the middle fossa dura, reaching foramen rotundum, so it is not a cavernous nerve in the strict sense. Know both counts for exams; surgically, V2 marks the inferior limit of the lateral cavernous exposure.

Adenoma invasion is graded on coronal MRI with [[c.knosp]]. Cavernous bleeding is low-pressure: head up, hemostatic matrix, cottonoid, patience. Packing too hard can compress CN VI or push material into the sinus.

structures.name: Medial wall of the cavernous sinus
structures.what: Thin meningeal dural layer separating the pituitary from the cavernous sinus, anchored to the ICA and sella by parasellar ligaments.
structures.why: It is the barrier adenomas cross; in functional adenomas it can be mobilized and resected (cutting the caroticoclinoid and parasellar ligaments) to raise remission rates.
structures.endo: Right, 30°, through the sellar opening: the glistening lateral boundary of the sella, pulsating with the cavernous ICA behind it.

structures.name: Internal carotid artery
structures.what: Main artery to the anterior brain and eye, ascending from the neck through the petrous bone and cavernous sinus to its intracranial bifurcation; it bulges into the lateral and posterior sphenoid walls.
structures.why: It is the structure whose injury defines catastrophe in endonasal surgery. Know its position on CT for every case.

rel.note: clinoid and ophthalmic segments lie inferolateral to the nerve
parapharyngeal segment lies posterolateral to the ET cartilage
the lacerum segment runs above its fibrocartilage

structures.ct: Axial and coronal bone windows: trace the carotid canal from the skull base (petrous, horizontal) to the foramen lacerum, up the paraclival groove, through the parasellar sulcus and under the anterior clinoid. Note dehiscence, medial loops and intercarotid distance.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: the carotid prominences; after bone removal a white, pulsating tube covered by periosteum and venous plexus.

pearls.text: On every sinus CT, look for the ICA in the sphenoid lateral wall and whether bone covers it.
A septum inserting on the carotid prominence is a warning, not a handle.

Endoscopic segments (Labib/Kassam, [[c.ica-endoscopic-segments]]): parapharyngeal, petrous, paraclival, parasellar, paraclinoid, intradural. Classic (Bouthillier): C1 cervical, C2 petrous, C3 lacerum, C4 cavernous, C5 clinoid, C6 ophthalmic, C7 communicating.

structures.name: Meningohypophyseal trunk
structures.what: Branch from the posterior bend of the cavernous ICA giving the tentorial, dorsal meningeal (clival) and inferior hypophyseal arteries.
structures.why: It feeds clival and petroclival tumors (chordoma, meningioma) and is torn during posterior compartment dissection; a torn branch bleeds from the ICA wall.

rel.note: via the dorsal meningeal artery to clival dura

structures.name: Inferolateral trunk
syn: artery of the inferior cavernous sinus
structures.what: Branch from the lateral side of the horizontal cavernous ICA supplying the cavernous cranial nerves and the trigeminal ganglion.
structures.why: It anastomoses with internal maxillary branches (a route for embolic material and for tumor supply) and can be avulsed during lateral compartment dissection, causing nerve ischemia and ICA bleeding.

structures.name: Proximal dural ring
structures.what: Thin dural collar from the lower surface of the anterior clinoid around the ICA, marking the top of the cavernous sinus and the start of the clinoid segment.
structures.why: It is incomplete and loosely attached, so venous plexus bleeds around it; it is the lower boundary of the paraclinoid segment exposed by drilling the lOCR.

structures.name: Distal dural ring
structures.what: Firm dural ring where the ICA becomes intradural, formed by dura from the upper clinoid surface continuing medially to the tuberculum and middle clinoid.
structures.why: Above it the ICA is in CSF (subarachnoid) — an injury here bleeds into the cisterns; medially a small pouch (carotid cave) can hide aneurysms that mimic intrasellar lesions.

structures.name: Oculomotor nerve
structures.what: Cranial nerve III: from the interpeduncular fossa between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, through the cavernous roof and upper lateral wall, to the orbit via the superior orbital fissure.
structures.why: It is the upper nerve at risk in the superior cavernous compartment and in retrosellar/interpeduncular work; injury gives ptosis, a down-and-out eye and a dilated pupil.

structures.name: Trochlear nerve
structures.what: Cranial nerve IV: the thinnest nerve, from the dorsal midbrain around the tentorial edge into the cavernous lateral wall below CN III, to the superior oblique via the superior orbital fissure.
structures.why: Being thin and in the lateral wall, it is rarely seen endonasally and injured by lateral compartment work; palsy gives vertical diplopia worse on looking down and in.

structures.name: Ophthalmic nerve
syn: ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
structures.what: First trigeminal division: from the ganglion forward in the lower lateral cavernous wall to the superior orbital fissure (lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves).
structures.why: Injury gives forehead and corneal numbness (neurotrophic keratopathy risk); with V2 it frames the lateral cavernous wall seen in transpterygoid work.

structures.name: Abducens nerve
structures.what: Cranial nerve VI: it leaves the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, climbs behind the clivus, turns forward over the petrous apex and runs inside the cavernous sinus beside the ICA to the lateral rectus muscle.
structures.why: It is the nerve most often injured in endonasal clival and cavernous surgery because it runs behind the paraclival ICA and inside the sinus; palsy gives horizontal diplopia (failure of abduction).

pearls.text: Check lateral gaze after any clival or cavernous case: VI is the nerve most at risk.

Endonasally the nerve is at risk at three points: the dural porus on the midclivus (lateral dural incisions), the gulfar segment behind the upper paraclival ICA near the petrous apex, and the cavernous segment lateral to the ICA (the upper edge of the quadrangular space). Stimulation mapping helps before opening dura lateral to midline.

structures.name: Dorello's canal
structures.what: Channel at the petroclival junction, within the petroclival venous confluence and roofed by the petrosphenoidal (Gruber) ligament, through which CN VI passes from the basilar plexus into the cavernous sinus.
structures.why: It is where the nerve is fixed and most easily stretched or compressed — by tumor, by packing, or by retraction around the paraclival ICA and petrous apex.

rel.note: deep to the upper paraclival segment in the endonasal view

structures.name: Petrosphenoidal ligament
structures.what: Fibrous band from the petrous apex to the lateral dorsum sellae forming the roof of Dorello's canal.
structures.why: It is the anatomical roof over CN VI at the petroclival junction; the nerve lies directly beneath it.

structures.name: Meckel's cave
structures.what: Dural pouch evaginating from the posterior fossa over the petrous apex, holding the trigeminal roots, cistern and ganglion, posterolateral to the cavernous sinus.
structures.why: Schwannomas, meningiomas, perineural spread (adenoid cystic carcinoma, SCC along V2/V3) and lesions of the petrous apex reach it; endonasally it is entered through the quadrangular space.

structures.name: Trigeminal ganglion
structures.what: Sensory ganglion of CN V in Meckel's cave giving V1, V2 and V3.
structures.why: Surgery in the quadrangular space works under or beside it; V2 is the lateral anchor that leads you back to it.

structures.name: Quadrangular space
structures.what: Endonasal window bounded medially by the paraclival ICA, inferiorly by the horizontal petrous ICA, superiorly by CN VI in the cavernous sinus and laterally by V2.
structures.why: It is the anteromedial corridor into Meckel's cave; its borders are the ICA on two sides and a nerve on each of the others, so you enter only after skeletonizing the ICA via the vidian canal.

rel.note: the paraclival segment is its medial border; the petrous segment its floor

structures.endo: Left, 0°, via transpterygoid corridor: after drilling the pterygoid base along the vidian canal, the rectangle of dura between the vertical and horizontal ICA, V2 and the course of CN VI.

structures.name: Optic nerve
structures.what: Cranial nerve II, a white-matter tract in a dural sheath running from the globe through the orbit and optic canal to the chiasm; segments are intraocular, intraorbital, intracanalicular and intracranial (cisternal).
structures.why: It is the structure most at risk in posterior ethmoid and sphenoid surgery (Onodi cell, dehiscent canal) and the one decompressed or protected in every suprasellar approach. Blindness from sinus surgery is usually a failure to know where it runs.

rel.note: within the canal the artery lies inferior (usually inferolateral) to the nerve
supraclinoid ICA lies inferolateral to the intracranial nerve
intracanalicular segment in the superolateral sinus wall

structures.ct: Axial and coronal: follow the nerve from the orbital apex into the canal; classify its relation to the sphenoid and posterior ethmoid ([[c.delano-optic-nerve]]) and check for an Onodi cell.
structures.endo: Right, 0°: seen as the optic prominence in the sphenoid or Onodi lateral wall; intracranially, through a transtuberculum opening, as a flat white band entering the canal under the falciform ligament.

pearls.text: If a cell above and lateral to the sphenoid contains the optic prominence, it is an Onodi cell ([[v.sphenoethmoidal-cell]]) — the nerve is in its wall.
Monopolar cautery, heat from a drill without irrigation, and pressure on a dehiscent canal are the three ways to injure it without cutting it.

Approximate segment lengths: intraocular ~1 mm, intraorbital ~25 mm ([[m.optic-nerve-intraorbital-length]]), intracanalicular ~ the canal length ([[m.optic-canal-length]]), intracranial variable with chiasm position.

structures.name: Optic chiasm
structures.what: Crossing of the nasal retinal fibers of both optic nerves, above the diaphragma sellae and in front of the pituitary stalk.
structures.why: Upward compression by a pituitary tumor causes bitemporal hemianopia. Its position (normal, prefixed, postfixed) decides whether the prechiasmatic or retrochiasmatic corridor is available endonasally.
structures.ct: MRI coronal T2: the flat X above the sella; look for upward displacement and thinning by tumor.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°, via transtuberculum: the white transverse band behind the tuberculum, with superior hypophyseal branches entering its undersurface.

pearls.text: A prefixed chiasm ([[v.prefixed-chiasm]]) leaves almost no prechiasmatic window; a postfixed chiasm ([[v.postfixed-chiasm]]) opens it but puts the chiasm over the dorsum.

structures.name: Optic tract
structures.what: Posterolateral continuation of the chiasm around the cerebral peduncle to the lateral geniculate body.
structures.why: Retrochiasmatic tumors (craniopharyngioma) displace the tracts laterally; tract injury gives a homonymous field cut.

structures.name: Falciform ligament
structures.what: Dural fold roofing the intracranial end of the optic canal, running from the anterior clinoid medially over the optic nerve.
structures.why: Tumors push the nerve up against its sharp edge; opening it (with the medial canal) is part of decompressing the nerve in tuberculum meningioma surgery.

structures.name: Ophthalmic artery
structures.what: First major intradural branch of the ICA, arising just above the distal dural ring under the optic nerve and entering the orbit through the optic canal below the nerve.
structures.why: It is the artery at risk when the optic sheath is incised or the inferior canal is drilled during decompression; its loss can cause blindness. The central retinal artery arises from it in the orbit.

pearls.text: Incise the optic sheath, if at all, along its superomedial aspect to stay away from the artery below it.
Origin is occasionally extradural from the clinoid segment ([[v.ophthalmic-artery-extradural-origin]]), placing it within the lOCR drilling field.

In the canal it lies inferolateral to the nerve in most patients and inferomedial in a minority (about 85% and 15% in one textbook account); the inferomedial artery sits where an endonasal decompression works, one more reason to incise the sheath superomedially.

structures.name: Superior hypophyseal artery
structures.what: One or more small branches from the medial side of the supraclinoid (ophthalmic segment) ICA running medially to the stalk, the undersurface of the chiasm and the proximal optic nerves.
structures.why: They are the chiasm's main inferior blood supply; sacrificing them (mistaken for tumor feeders) can cause visual loss even when the nerves are untouched.

structures.name: Suprasellar cistern
structures.what: CSF space above the diaphragma sellae containing the optic chiasm, stalk and the supraclinoid ICA branches.
structures.why: Opening it (diaphragmatic tear or deliberate transtuberculum dural opening) creates a high-flow CSF leak that must be closed with a multilayer, usually vascularized, repair.

structures.name: Liliequist's membrane
structures.what: Arachnoid sheet from the dorsum sellae to the mammillary bodies separating the chiasmatic cistern from the interpeduncular and prepontine cisterns.
structures.why: Opening it from in front exposes the basilar apex, P1s and CN III in retrosellar and retroinfundibular approaches.

structures.name: Interpeduncular cistern
structures.what: CSF space between the cerebral peduncles behind Liliequist's membrane, containing the basilar apex, the P1 segments with their perforators, and the origins of CN III.
structures.why: It is the target of transdorsum (pituitary transposition) approaches for retroinfundibular craniopharyngiomas and upper clival tumors; its thalamoperforators are unforgiving.

structures.name: Hypothalamus
structures.what: Diencephalic floor and lower walls of the third ventricle, from the chiasm back to the mammillary bodies, from which the stalk descends.
structures.why: Craniopharyngiomas adhere to it; injury causes obesity, thermal and sleep dysregulation, memory and behavioral change. The degree of hypothalamic involvement is a stop point for radical resection.

structures.name: Mammillary bodies
structures.what: Paired rounded eminences at the back of the hypothalamic floor, in front of the interpeduncular fossa.
structures.why: They are the posterior landmark of the third-ventricular floor and the upper attachment of Liliequist's membrane in retroinfundibular dissection.

structures.name: Lamina terminalis
structures.what: Thin membrane forming the anterior wall of the third ventricle from the upper chiasm to the anterior commissure.
structures.why: It is the window to the third ventricle above the chiasm for retrochiasmatic and intraventricular craniopharyngioma extensions, with the ACoA complex in front of it.

structures.name: Anterior cerebral artery
structures.what: Medial terminal branch of the ICA: the A1 segment runs medially above the optic nerve or chiasm to the ACoA; the A2 ascends in the interhemispheric fissure in front of the lamina terminalis.
structures.why: Planum and tuberculum meningiomas and craniopharyngiomas push the A1s and A2s up and back; they and their perforators must be dissected off the tumor capsule under vision.

rel.note: A1 crosses above the optic nerve or chiasm

structures.name: Anterior communicating artery
structures.what: Short artery joining the two A1–A2 junctions above the chiasm or optic nerves, in front of the lamina terminalis.
structures.why: Its perforators (including the subcallosal artery) supply the hypothalamus, fornix and chiasm; injury causes memory and personality change. It sits at the upper limit of transplanum exposure.

structures.name: Recurrent artery of Heubner
structures.what: Branch usually from the proximal A2 near the ACoA that doubles back along the A1 to enter the anterior perforated substance.
structures.why: It runs over the A1 in the transplanum field and supplies the caudate head and anterior internal capsule; its loss causes contralateral face and arm weakness.

structures.name: Posterior communicating artery
structures.what: Branch from the posterior wall of the supraclinoid ICA running posteromedially above CN III to join the posterior cerebral artery.
structures.why: Its anterior thalamoperforators are at risk in retroinfundibular and interpeduncular dissection; it marks the lateral wall of the retrosellar corridor.

structures.name: Clivus
structures.what: Sloping midline bone from the dorsum sellae down to the anterior rim of the foramen magnum (basion), formed by the sphenoid body above and the basiocciput below.
structures.why: It separates the sphenoid sinus and nasopharynx from the brainstem and basilar artery; chordomas and chondrosarcomas arise here, and transclival approaches drill through it between the paraclival ICAs.
structures.ct: Sagittal: the long oblique bone from the sella to the foramen magnum; divided endonasally into thirds by the sellar floor and sphenoid floor.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°: the clival recess of the sphenoid (middle third) and, below the sphenoid floor, the bone behind the nasopharyngeal mucosa, pharyngobasilar fascia and longus capitis (lower third).

pearls.text: Upper third = dorsum sellae; middle third = sellar floor to sphenoid floor; lower third = sphenoid floor to foramen magnum (endonasal definition, [[c.clivus-thirds]]).
The basilar plexus lies between the clival bone and dura; CN VI pierces the dura at the midclivus a short distance lateral to midline, so clival dura is opened in the midline and extended with care.

Clival marrow changes with age: hematopoietic marrow gives low-to-intermediate T1 signal in children and young adults, and the signal brightens as fat replaces it. A dark clivus can be normal in a young patient, so judge a "lesion" against the age-expected signal.

structures.name: Basilar venous plexus
structures.what: Network of venous channels between the periosteal and meningeal layers of the clival dura, connecting the cavernous sinuses, inferior petrosal sinuses and marginal sinus.
structures.why: It bleeds heavily when the clival dura is exposed; control with hemostatic matrix, gentle pressure and patience, not cautery that shrinks the dura and endangers CN VI, which runs within it.

structures.name: Basilar artery
structures.what: Midline artery formed by the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction, ascending in front of the pons behind the clivus to divide into the posterior cerebral arteries.
structures.why: It lies directly behind the clival dura; its pontine perforators to the brainstem are the limiting structure of transclival tumor dissection.
structures.endo: Midline, 0°, after clival dural opening: the large pulsating trunk in the prepontine cistern with AICA and pontine perforators leaving it.

pearls.text: Chordoma dissection stops at the arachnoid over the basilar; perforator injury gives brainstem infarction even when the trunk is intact.

structures.name: Posterior cerebral artery
structures.what: Terminal branch of the basilar artery; the P1 segment runs laterally above CN III to the PCoA junction, giving thalamoperforators.
structures.why: P1 perforators to the midbrain and thalamus are at risk at the basilar apex in transdorsum and interpeduncular work.

structures.name: Superior cerebellar artery
structures.what: Branch of the upper basilar just below its apex, passing under CN III around the brainstem below the tentorium.
structures.why: With the PCA it brackets CN III; it is seen in upper clival and interpeduncular exposures.

structures.name: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
structures.what: Branch of the lower or middle basilar coursing laterally across the pons toward the cerebellopontine angle, closely related to CN VI.
structures.why: In midclival approaches it crosses near the abducens nerve and is dissected off chordoma capsule; its labyrinthine branch supplies the inner ear.

rel.note: crosses close to the cisternal segment

structures.name: Vertebral artery
structures.what: Artery ascending through the cervical transverse foramina, around the C1 lateral mass, through the dura at the foramen magnum and along the anterolateral medulla to join its partner as the basilar artery.
structures.why: It is the lateral limit of lower clival, transcondylar and odontoid exposures; the intradural V4 and PICA lie behind the lower clival dura.

rel.note: the two vertebrals unite to form it

structures.name: Pons
structures.what: Middle part of the brainstem, lying behind the basilar artery and the middle clivus.
structures.why: It is the deep boundary of every transclival dissection; brainstem injury, not the ICA, is often what limits resection of clival chordoma.

structures.name: Prepontine cistern
structures.what: CSF space between the clival dura and the pons, containing the basilar artery, AICA origins and the cisternal CN VI.
structures.why: Opening it creates a high-flow posterior fossa leak, the hardest endonasal defect to seal; plan a vascularized flap and consider lumbar drainage.

structures.name: Foramen lacerum
structures.what: Fibrocartilage-filled gap at the junction of the sphenoid body, petrous apex and basiocciput, over which the ICA turns up from its petrous to its paraclival course.
structures.why: It is where the vidian canal ends and the ICA's anterior genu sits: the vidian nerve leads you to it, and it is the hinge between the petrous and paraclival segments.
structures.ct: Axial at the level of the vidian canal: the ragged gap at the petrous apex tip, medial to the anterior genu of the carotid canal.

pearls.text: Apart from small meningeal branches and emissary veins nothing major traverses the foramen lacerum; the ICA passes over it, not through it, and the vidian nerve forms at its upper margin.

structures.name: Petrous apex
syn: apex of the petrous temporal bone
structures.what: Medial tip of the petrous temporal bone, anteromedial to the inner ear and internal auditory canal, between the petrous ICA, the clivus and Meckel's cave.
structures.why: Cholesterol granulomas, mucoceles, chondrosarcomas and apicitis live here; lesions that bulge medially toward the sphenoid can be drained endonasally medial to the paraclival ICA.

rel.note: petrous segment anterolaterally, paraclival segment anteriorly
posterolateral, behind the paraclival ICA; reached through the sinus in the [[p.medial-petrous-apex-approach]]

structures.ct: Axial bone window: the triangle medial to the cochlea and IAC; compare sides for asymmetric pneumatization or marrow before calling a lesion. MRI (T1 bright, T2 bright, no enhancement) identifies cholesterol granuloma.

pearls.text: Asymmetric marrow or pneumatization is the commonest "lesion" of the petrous apex on imaging; do not operate on a leave-alone variant.

structures.name: Petrous carotid canal
structures.what: Bony canal within the petrous temporal bone carrying the petrous ICA from its entrance at the skull base, forward and medially, to the foramen lacerum, where the artery turns up into its paraclival course.
structures.why: It is the surgeon's guide to the horizontal petrous ICA before it is skeletonized: the vidian canal runs anteromedial and roughly parallel to it toward the same point at the foramen lacerum, so following the vidian nerve back leads onto the canal's anteromedial wall in the infrapetrous and transpterygoid corridors.

rel.note: the canal opens anteromedially into it, where the ICA turns into the paraclival segment

the vidian canal runs straight back through the sphenoid floor and meets the carotid canal at the foramen lacerum (anterior genu); the ICA lies superolateral to the vidian canal's posterior end, so drilling follows the canal's inferomedial side

structures.ct: Axial bone window: follow the canal from its opening on the inferior petrous surface through the vertical segment and genu, then anteromedially along the horizontal segment to the foramen lacerum. Coronal: the vidian canal in the sphenoid floor leads back to the same point.

structures.name: Petroclival synchondrosis
structures.what: Cartilaginous joint between the petrous apex and the clivus, running from the foramen lacerum back to the jugular foramen.
structures.why: It is the typical origin of chondrosarcoma (paramedian), in contrast to chordoma (midline); the inferior petrosal sinus runs along it.

rel.note: posterolateral, beyond the paraclival ICA — where chondrosarcoma arises

structures.name: Inferior petrosal sinus
structures.what: Dural sinus from the posterior cavernous sinus along the petroclival synchondrosis to the jugular bulb, receiving the basilar plexus.
structures.why: It is the main outflow of the cavernous sinus and pituitary, sampled bilaterally (IPSS) to lateralize ACTH secretion in Cushing disease; it bleeds in petroclival dissection.

structures.name: Greater superficial petrosal nerve
structures.what: Parasympathetic branch of the facial nerve from the geniculate ganglion running anteromedially under the middle fossa dura, above the horizontal petrous ICA, to the foramen lacerum, where it joins the deep petrosal nerve to form the vidian nerve.
structures.why: It is the reason the vidian nerve points to the ICA: both run to the anterior genu; it also explains dry eye after vidian sacrifice.

rel.note: it continues forward as the vidian nerve

structures.name: Foramen magnum
structures.what: Large opening in the occipital bone transmitting the medulla, vertebral arteries and spinal accessory roots; its anterior rim is the basion.
structures.why: It is the inferior end of the transclival corridor; the basion and odontoid tip define the target in transodontoid surgery.

structures.name: Occipital condyle
structures.what: Paired articular process beside the foramen magnum articulating with C1; the hypoglossal canal runs above its junction with the jugular tubercle.
structures.why: Drilling its medial part (far-medial, transcondylar) widens the lower clival exposure but risks the hypoglossal nerve and craniocervical stability.

structures.name: Hypoglossal canal
structures.what: Canal through the occipital bone above the occipital condyle transmitting CN XII.
structures.why: It limits lateral drilling of the condyle in far-medial approaches; identify it on CT and stop medial to it.

structures.name: Hypoglossal nerve
structures.what: Cranial nerve XII, from the preolivary sulcus through the hypoglossal canal to the tongue.
structures.why: Injury during transcondylar extension gives ipsilateral tongue weakness and, with other lower cranial nerve deficits, swallowing problems.

structures.name: Odontoid process
structures.what: Upward peg of C2 articulating with the back of the C1 anterior arch, held by the transverse ligament, with apical and alar ligaments to the basion and condyles.
structures.why: Basilar invagination and inflammatory pannus compress the medulla here; the endonasal transodontoid route removes it from the front without splitting the palate.

rel.note: tip normally just below the basion

structures.name: Anterior arch of the atlas
structures.what: Front of the C1 ring, lying in front of the dens, with the anterior tubercle for the longus colli.
structures.why: It is the first bone met below the clivus in transodontoid surgery; removing it (or its middle part) exposes the dens.

structures.name: Transverse ligament of the atlas
structures.what: Strong band between the C1 lateral masses passing behind the dens.
structures.why: It is the main C1–C2 stabilizer; its removal with the dens and C1 arch usually commits the patient to posterior fusion.

structures.name: Tectorial membrane
structures.what: Upward continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament from the C2 body to the inner clivus, behind the transverse ligament.
structures.why: It is the last layer before dura in transodontoid decompression; keeping it intact avoids a CSF leak.

structures.name: Anterior atlanto-occipital membrane
structures.what: Membrane from the upper C1 anterior arch to the anterior rim of the foramen magnum, deep to the longus capitis.
structures.why: It is incised between clivus and C1 to reach the dens tip and basion.

structures.name: Longus capitis
structures.what: Prevertebral muscle from the cervical transverse processes to the inferior surface of the basiocciput, lateral to the pharyngeal tubercle.
structures.why: It is elevated or resected with the pharyngobasilar fascia to expose the lower clivus; a flap of it can buttress lower clival reconstruction.

structures.name: Longus colli
structures.what: Prevertebral muscle on the front of the cervical spine inserting on the anterior tubercle of C1.
structures.why: It is detached from the C1 tubercle to expose the anterior arch and dens.

structures.name: Pharyngobasilar fascia
structures.what: Tough fibrous layer under the nasopharyngeal mucosa anchoring the pharynx to the pharyngeal tubercle of the clivus and to the petrous apex.
structures.why: It is incised (often as part of an inferiorly based nasopharyngeal flap) to reach the lower clivus; laterally it covers the Eustachian tube and the parapharyngeal ICA, so incisions stay medial to the ET.

rel.note: the ET cartilage passes through its upper lateral part

landmarks.name: Sphenoid ostium (center)
landmarks.locate: Center of the natural ostium on the anterior sphenoid wall, in the sphenoethmoidal recess medial to the superior turbinate.

landmarks.name: Choanal arch (superior choanal margin)
landmarks.locate: Highest midpoint of the choanal rim on the same side, where the vomer ala meets the sphenoid body.

landmarks.name: Tuberculum sellae (midline point)
landmarks.locate: Midline crest of the tuberculum where the chiasmatic sulcus turns down into the anterior sellar wall.

landmarks.name: Sellar floor (deepest midline point)
landmarks.locate: Lowest midline point of the hypophyseal fossa on the sagittal plane.

landmarks.name: Dorsum sellae (top midline point)
landmarks.locate: Uppermost midline point of the dorsum sellae.

landmarks.name: Pituitary gland upper surface
landmarks.locate: Highest point of the gland's upper surface on the midline coronal section, used with the sellar floor for gland height.

landmarks.name: Limbus sphenoidale (midline)
landmarks.locate: Midline point of the ridge at the posterior edge of the planum.

landmarks.name: Lateral opticocarotid recess (apex)
landmarks.locate: Deepest point of the recess between optic and carotid prominences on the superolateral sphenoid wall.

landmarks.name: Medial opticocarotid recess
landmarks.locate: Notch at the lateral end of the tuberculum where the medial optic canal meets the paraclinoid carotid prominence.

landmarks.name: Optic canal, intracranial opening
landmarks.locate: Center of the intracranial (posterior) opening of the canal, under the falciform ligament.

landmarks.name: Optic canal, orbital opening
landmarks.locate: Center of the orbital (anterior) opening of the canal at the annulus of Zinn.

landmarks.name: ICA, paraclinoid segment medial wall
landmarks.locate: Most medial point of the clinoid-segment ICA just below the distal dural ring; paired R/L instances define the narrowest intercarotid distance at this level.

landmarks.name: ICA, parasellar segment medial wall
landmarks.locate: Most medial point of the horizontal cavernous ICA beside the sella.

landmarks.name: ICA, paraclival segment medial wall
landmarks.locate: Most medial point of the vertical paraclival ICA at the level of the clival recess.

landmarks.name: ICA anterior genu (lacerum)
landmarks.locate: The turn from the horizontal petrous to the vertical paraclival ICA above the foramen lacerum, at the posterior end of the vidian canal.

landmarks.name: Vidian canal, posterior opening
landmarks.locate: Posterior end of the vidian canal at the anterior margin of the foramen lacerum.

landmarks.name: Sphenoid floor (midline)
landmarks.locate: Midline point of the sphenoid sinus floor on the sagittal plane; boundary between middle and lower clivus.

landmarks.name: Pharyngeal tubercle
landmarks.locate: Small midline bony tubercle on the inferior surface of the basiocciput, anterior to the foramen magnum, where the pharyngeal raphe attaches.

landmarks.name: Basion
landmarks.locate: Midline point on the anterior rim of the foramen magnum.

landmarks.name: Odontoid tip
landmarks.locate: Apex of the dens in the midline.

landmarks.name: Abducens dural porus
landmarks.locate: Point where CN VI pierces the inner (meningeal) layer of the clival dura at the midclivus, lateral to midline.

variants.name: Dehiscent ICA in the sphenoid sinus
variants.def: No bone between the ICA (usually parasellar or paraclival) and the sphenoid mucosa. CT: no bony margin over the carotid canal on thin-section bone windows — bone thinner than the slice resolution can mimic it.
variants.why: A dehiscent ICA can be opened by suction, a microdebrider or mucosal stripping. Leave mucosa over the prominence, keep powered instruments away, and warn the team preoperatively.

prev.note: Microsurgical dissection. Where bone was present it was frequently thinner than 0.5 mm, so "covered" does not mean protected.
CT series vary widely: thin bone below resolution reads as dehiscent, and series mix per-side and per-patient denominators.

variants.name: Dehiscent optic canal
variants.def: No bone between the optic nerve sheath and the mucosa of the sphenoid or an Onodi cell along the canal.
variants.why: The nerve is then protected only by mucosa and sheath: no suction, cautery or pressure on the optic prominence, and particular care when an Onodi cell carries the canal.

prev.note: CT over-calls dehiscence where bone is thinner than the slice; higher rates are reported when the nerve protrudes (DeLano types 2–3).

variants.name: Sphenoid septum inserting on the ICA
variants.def: The main intersinus septum or an accessory septum inserts posteriorly on the bony prominence of the paraclival or parasellar ICA. CT: axial slices show the septum meeting the carotid canal wall.
variants.why: Twisting or avulsing that septum can fracture the canal and tear the ICA. Cut it with through-cutting instruments or drill it flush, never rock it off.

prev.note: Counts any septation (main or accessory) inserting on the carotid prominence; the main septum alone inserts on the ICA far less often. Rates depend on counting any vs main septum and bony contact vs proximity.

variants.name: Protruding carotid prominence
variants.def: The carotid canal bulges into the sphenoid lumen: a visible prominence endoscopically, or on CT a canal projecting into the sinus (often defined as more than half its circumference surrounded by air).
variants.why: The more the ICA protrudes, the thinner its cover and the closer it is to a straight instrument path; protrusion goes with extensive (sellar/postsellar, lateral) pneumatization.

variants.name: Optic canal indenting the sphenoid (DeLano type 2)
variants.def: The optic canal bulges into the superolateral sphenoid wall as a prominence without being surrounded by air.
variants.why: The optic prominence is then a clear landmark but also a target: the canal wall is thin, often with an lOCR below it.

prev.note: Any visible optic protrusion into the sinus; broader definition than DeLano type 2.

variants.name: Optic nerve traversing the sphenoid (DeLano type 3)
variants.def: The optic canal runs through the sphenoid sinus, surrounded by air for at least half its circumference, often on a bony mesentery.
variants.why: The nerve is exposed on several sides and its canal is often dehiscent; a septum or mesentery attaching to it must not be twisted.

variants.name: Pneumatized anterior clinoid process
variants.def: Air within the anterior clinoid continuous with the sphenoid, usually via a pneumatized optic strut (deep lOCR). CT: air in the clinoid on coronal and axial bone windows.
variants.why: It deepens the lOCR and places the optic nerve and clinoid ICA on thin bone in the sinus wall; it is associated with protruding and dehiscent optic canals.

prev.note: DeLano's CT series, where most pneumatized clinoids accompanied type 2 or 3 optic nerves. Other CT series report wider ranges, depending on population and whether strut-only pneumatization is counted.

variants.name: Laterally pneumatized sphenoid (lateral recess)
variants.def: Sphenoid air extending lateral to the line between the vidian canal and foramen rotundum, into the greater wing and/or pterygoid base.
variants.why: Puts V2 and the vidian nerve in relief in the sinus wall and thins the middle fossa floor (spontaneous CSF leak site). Reaching it needs a contralateral angled view or a transpterygoid approach. One textbook account puts lateral pneumatization into the pterygoid base at about 35% of people, bilateral in about 17% (method not stated).

variants.name: Conchal sphenoid
variants.def: Rudimentary sphenoid sinus separated from the sella by a thick block of cancellous bone; no pneumatization under the sella.
variants.why: No prominences to guide you: the sella is reached by drilling through solid bone under navigation, staying midline between the (unseen) ICAs. Normal in young children.

prev.note: Anatomical-radiographic series predating CT; rarer still in microsurgical cadaver series.

variants.name: Presellar sphenoid
variants.def: Pneumatization reaches but does not pass the coronal plane of the anterior sellar wall; the sella lies behind and above the sinus.
variants.why: The sellar floor must be reached by drilling posteriorly through the sinus's posterior wall; the carotid prominences are faint or absent.

prev.note: Different series and definitions of the anterior sellar plane explain the spread.

variants.name: Postsellar sphenoid
variants.def: Pneumatization extends behind the coronal plane of the posterior sellar wall into the dorsum and clivus.
variants.why: Gives a wide sellar and clival window, but thins the bone over the paraclival ICAs and can pneumatize the dorsum; the sella looks like a free-standing bulge.

variants.name: Cavernous ICA indenting the pituitary
variants.def: The cavernous ICA bulges through the medial cavernous wall into the sella, indenting the lateral surface of the gland.
variants.why: Lateral curettage inside the sella can strike the ICA directly; use Doppler and blunt ring curettes and keep lateral sweeps gentle.

variants.name: Kissing carotids
variants.def: The two ICAs meet or nearly meet in the midline — in the sella or the sphenoid sinus — leaving a very narrow or no intercarotid window. Ectatic ICAs in acromegaly narrow the window similarly.
variants.why: A transsphenoidal opening may be unsafe or must be tailored to the available window; demand CTA or MRA and use Doppler before every bony or dural opening.

variants.name: Prefixed optic chiasm
variants.def: The chiasm lies over the tuberculum sellae rather than the diaphragma, with short intracranial optic nerves.
variants.why: The prechiasmatic window is tiny: suprasellar lesions must be reached below or behind the chiasm, and the chiasm is exposed immediately on opening tuberculum dura.

prev.note: Smaller microsurgical series; criteria for "normal" differ slightly.

variants.name: Postfixed optic chiasm
variants.def: The chiasm lies over the dorsum sellae, with long intracranial optic nerves.
variants.why: A wide prechiasmatic window favors the transtuberculum corridor, but pituitary tumors compress the optic nerves rather than the chiasm and the stalk lies under the chiasm.

variants.name: Sella turcica bridge (interclinoid ossification)
variants.def: Ossification of the interclinoid ligament joining anterior and posterior clinoids over the sella, seen on lateral radiograph or sagittal CT.
variants.why: Endonasally mostly a radiographic curiosity; it stiffens the lateral sellar roof and matters in posterior clinoidectomy and transcranial anterior clinoidectomy.

variants.name: Caroticoclinoid foramen
variants.def: Ossified caroticoclinoid ligament between the anterior and middle clinoid processes, enclosing the clinoid ICA in a bony ring.
variants.why: Drilling at the mOCR is then next to a complete bony ring around the ICA; thin it with a fine diamond bur under irrigation or leave it.

variants.name: Empty sella
variants.def: The sella is largely filled with CSF and the gland flattened against the floor (partial or complete): primary, from arachnoid herniation through the diaphragm, or secondary after surgery, radiation or apoplexy.
variants.why: Primary empty sella goes with raised intracranial pressure and spontaneous CSF leaks; any transsellar surgery through it carries a high risk of leak, so reconstruction is planned in advance.

variants.name: Persistent trigeminal artery
variants.def: Persistent embryonic carotid–basilar anastomosis from the cavernous ICA running back to the basilar artery, lateral (along the trigeminal root) or medial (through the sella or dorsum) in course.
variants.why: The medial, intrasellar course crosses the pituitary fossa and can be torn during transsellar surgery; recognize it on preoperative MRA or CTA.

prev.note: Pooled angiographic and MR-angiographic series; the share taking a medial (transsellar or transdorsal) course varies between series.

variants.name: V2 protruding into the lateral recess
variants.def: The foramen rotundum canal forms a ridge in the lateral recess wall, with thin or dehiscent bone.
variants.why: A landmark for the lateral recess and PPF, but lateral recess work can cause V2 numbness; CSF leaks lateral to it need a transpterygoid route.

variants.name: Vidian canal protruding into the sphenoid floor
variants.def: The vidian canal is raised into the sinus floor on a bony ridge or septum, typically with lateral or pterygoid pneumatization.
variants.why: Easy to follow back to the anterior genu of the ICA, but also easy to injure while flattening the floor (dry eye).

variants.name: Medialized (retropharyngeal) ICA
variants.def: Tortuous or medially displaced cervical (parapharyngeal) ICA lying close to the posterior pharyngeal wall, visible on axial CT or MRI.
variants.why: Nasopharyngeal incisions for lower clival and transodontoid approaches must stay medial to it; check the axial images at C1–C2 before planning the flap.

variants.name: Sphenoid ostium lateral to the superior turbinate
variants.def: The natural sphenoid ostium opens lateral to (behind) the superior turbinate rather than medial to it.
variants.why: The ostium is not seen in the SER until the inferior superior turbinate is resected or lateralized; do not mistake a posterior ethmoid opening for it.

prev.note: The ostium was medial to the superior turbinate in the remainder.

variants.name: Large anterior intercavernous sinus
variants.def: The anterior intercavernous sinus is wide and covers much or all of the anterior sellar dura; with the posterior sinus it may form a complete "circular sinus".
variants.why: Dural opening bleeds briskly: open low, coagulate the dural edges with bipolar, and use hemostatic matrix with gentle pressure.

variants.name: Extradural ophthalmic artery origin
variants.def: The ophthalmic artery arises from the clinoid (C5) or cavernous ICA below the distal dural ring instead of from the intradural ICA.
variants.why: Its origin then lies in the drilling field of the lOCR/optic strut during optic canal decompression.

classifications.name: Sphenoid pneumatization (sagittal type)
classifications.basis: How far pneumatization extends back under the sella, judged against coronal planes through the anterior and posterior sellar walls (Hammer and Radberg; postsellar subtype from later anatomic and CT work).

classes.label: Conchal
classes.criterion: Rudimentary sinus separated from the sella by thick cancellous bone.
classes.why: Drill through solid bone under navigation.

classes.label: Presellar
classes.criterion: Air reaches but does not pass the plane of the anterior sellar wall.
classes.why: Sella lies behind the sinus; prominences faint.

classes.label: Sellar
classes.criterion: Air extends under the sella to the plane of the posterior sellar wall.
classes.why: The standard, most favorable configuration.

classes.label: Postsellar
classes.criterion: Air extends behind the plane of the posterior sellar wall into the dorsum and clivus.
classes.why: Wide window; thin bone over the paraclival ICAs.

classifications.caveats: The original three types predate CT; "postsellar" subdivides the old sellar type. Lateral extensions (lateral recess, anterior clinoid, pterygoid) are scored separately. Young children are normally conchal or presellar. Sources differ in terms: textbook chapters using a three-type scheme call the dominant type "sellar" or "postsellar" interchangeably (air under the whole sella) and quote roughly 5–10% conchal, 25–30% presellar and about 65% sellar/postsellar — a conchal figure higher than the older anatomical series ([[v.conchal-sphenoid]]). Check which scheme a figure uses before comparing it.

classifications.name: ICA endoscopic endonasal segments
classifications.basis: Six segments named for the ventral skull base landmarks the surgeon sees endonasally (Labib et al. 2014).

classes.label: Parapharyngeal
classes.criterion: Cervical ICA from the bifurcation to the external carotid canal opening, in the parapharyngeal space posterolateral to the Eustachian tube.
classes.why: At risk in lower clival, transodontoid and infratemporal work; the ET cartilage is its guide.

classes.label: Petrous
classes.criterion: Within the carotid canal: a short vertical part, then the horizontal part running anteromedially to the anterior genu above the foramen lacerum.
classes.why: Reached along the vidian canal in transpterygoid approaches; forms the floor of the quadrangular space.

classes.label: Paraclival
classes.criterion: Vertical segment from the foramen lacerum up the side of the clival recess to the posterior bend of the cavernous ICA; its lower end sits over the foramen lacerum, and laterally it faces the quadrangular space and Meckel's cave.
classes.why: Lateral limit of transclival work and medial border of the quadrangular space; CN VI lies deep to its upper part.

classes.label: Parasellar
classes.criterion: Within the cavernous sinus beside the sella, from the posterior bend through the horizontal segment to the anterior bend.
classes.why: Lateral limit of the sellar opening; adenoma invasion is graded against it.

classes.label: Paraclinoid
classes.criterion: Between the proximal and distal dural rings under the anterior clinoid, seen endonasally beneath the lOCR and lateral to the mOCR.
classes.why: Lateral limit of the transtuberculum opening; drilling the optic strut exposes it.

classes.label: Intradural
classes.criterion: Above the distal dural ring to the bifurcation, giving the ophthalmic, superior hypophyseal, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries.
classes.why: Seen through transtuberculum dural openings; bleeding enters the subarachnoid space.

classifications.caveats: Endoscopic segments are landmark-based and do not map one-to-one onto the Bouthillier scheme: roughly, paraclival ≈ C3 plus the posterior vertical part of C4, parasellar ≈ the rest of C4, paraclinoid ≈ C5, intradural ≈ C6–C7.

classifications.name: ICA segments (Bouthillier C1–C7)
classifications.basis: Segments numbered in the direction of blood flow and named for the compartment each traverses (Bouthillier, van Loveren and Keller 1996).

classes.label: Cervical
classes.criterion: From the carotid bifurcation to the entry into the carotid canal.

classes.label: Petrous
classes.criterion: Within the carotid canal, from its entry to the posterior edge of the foramen lacerum.

classes.label: Lacerum
classes.criterion: From the end of the carotid canal, over the foramen lacerum, to the upper margin of the petrolingual ligament.

classes.label: Cavernous
classes.criterion: From the petrolingual ligament to the proximal dural ring.

classes.label: Clinoid
classes.criterion: Between the proximal and distal dural rings.

classes.label: Ophthalmic
classes.criterion: From the distal dural ring to the origin of the posterior communicating artery.

classes.label: Communicating
classes.criterion: From the posterior communicating artery origin to the terminal bifurcation.

classifications.caveats: The older Fischer numbering ran against blood flow (C1 terminal); check which system a paper uses. The petrolingual ligament is not an endonasal landmark, so endoscopic segment names are used at the table.

classifications.name: Optic nerve relation to the posterior sinuses (DeLano)
classifications.basis: CT relationship of the optic nerve to the sphenoid and posterior ethmoid sinuses (DeLano, Fun and Zinreich 1996).

classes.label: Type 1 — adjacent
