classes.criterion: Nerve runs next to the sphenoid sinus without indenting its wall.
classes.why: Most common; least exposed.

classes.label: Type 2 — indenting
classes.criterion: Nerve indents the sphenoid wall as a prominence.
classes.why: Clear optic prominence; thin canal.

classes.label: Type 3 — traversing
classes.criterion: Nerve passes through the sphenoid, surrounded by air for at least half its circumference.
classes.why: Highest risk; often dehiscent.

classes.label: Type 4 — posterior ethmoid
classes.criterion: Nerve runs immediately lateral to the posterior ethmoid (sphenoethmoidal) cell as well as the sphenoid.
classes.why: The nerve is in the lateral wall of an Onodi cell ([[v.sphenoethmoidal-cell]]).

classifications.caveats: Types 2 and 3 are associated with anterior clinoid pneumatization and with dehiscence. Classify each side separately.

classifications.name: Knosp classification of cavernous sinus invasion
classifications.basis: Coronal MRI extent of a pituitary adenoma relative to three lines between the supra- and intracavernous ICA: the medial tangent, the intercarotid (center) line and the lateral tangent (Knosp 1993; grade 3 split by Micko 2015).

classes.label: Grade 0
classes.criterion: Tumor does not pass the medial tangent.
classes.why: Cavernous invasion essentially absent.

classes.label: Grade 1
classes.criterion: Past the medial tangent but not the intercarotid line.
classes.why: Invasion rare (about 1.5% at endoscopic verification, Micko 2015).

classes.label: Grade 2
classes.criterion: Past the intercarotid line but not the lateral tangent.
classes.why: Invasion in about 10% (Micko 2015).

classes.label: Grade 3A
classes.criterion: Lateral to the lateral tangent, extending into the superior cavernous compartment.
classes.why: Invasion in about a quarter (Micko 2015).

classes.label: Grade 3B
classes.criterion: Lateral to the lateral tangent, extending into the inferior cavernous compartment.
classes.why: Invasion in about 70%; lower gross-total resection rates (Micko 2015).

classes.label: Grade 4
classes.criterion: Total encasement of the intracavernous ICA.
classes.why: Invasion essentially certain.

classifications.caveats: MRI grade estimates, not proves, invasion; true invasion is confirmed at surgery by breach of the medial cavernous wall.

classifications.name: Clival thirds (endonasal)
classifications.basis: Endonasal division of the clivus by sphenoid landmarks: the sellar floor and the sphenoid sinus floor (Kassam et al. 2005).

classes.label: Upper third
classes.criterion: Dorsum sellae and posterior clinoids, above the sellar floor.
classes.why: Reached by pituitary transposition or through the sella; targets the interpeduncular cistern and basilar apex.

classes.label: Middle third
classes.criterion: From the sellar floor to the sphenoid floor, between the paraclival ICAs (the clival recess).
classes.why: Opens onto the prepontine cistern and basilar trunk; CN VI pierces the dura here.

classes.label: Lower third
classes.criterion: From the sphenoid floor to the foramen magnum, behind the nasopharynx; the Eustachian tubes and parapharyngeal ICAs are lateral.
classes.why: Vertebrobasilar junction and lower cranial nerves; far-medial extensions via the condyles.

classifications.caveats: Transcranial descriptions divide the clivus by intracranial neural landmarks, which do not coincide exactly with these endonasal thirds.

classifications.name: Intraoperative CSF leak grade (Esposito–Kelly)
classifications.basis: Severity of intraoperative CSF leak during transsphenoidal surgery, tested with a Valsalva maneuver, used to grade the repair (Esposito et al. 2007).

classes.label: Grade 0
classes.criterion: No leak, confirmed with Valsalva.
classes.why: No leak repair needed beyond closing the sellar floor if desired.

classes.label: Grade 1
classes.criterion: Small "weeping" leak without an obvious diaphragmatic defect.
classes.why: Collagen or fascia inlay with or without a buttress.

classes.label: Grade 2
classes.criterion: Moderate leak with an obvious diaphragmatic defect.
classes.why: Fat graft plus buttress and onlay; consider a vascularized flap.

classes.label: Grade 3
classes.criterion: Large diaphragmatic or dural defect, as after extended (transplanum, transclival) approaches or third-ventricle entry.
classes.why: Multilayer repair with a vascularized nasoseptal flap; lumbar drain in high-risk defects.

classifications.caveats: Designed for pituitary surgery; extended approaches are grade 3 by definition. The original grade 3 repair (fat, buttress and lumbar drain) predates routine use of the nasoseptal flap.

classifications.name: Optic chiasm position
classifications.basis: Anteroposterior position of the chiasm relative to the sella (Bergland 1968; Renn and Rhoton 1975).

classes.label: Prefixed
classes.criterion: Chiasm over the tuberculum sellae.
classes.why: Little or no prechiasmatic window.

classes.label: Normal
classes.criterion: Chiasm over the diaphragma sellae.
classes.why: The usual configuration (most specimens).

classes.label: Postfixed
classes.criterion: Chiasm over the dorsum sellae.
classes.why: Wide prechiasmatic window; stalk under the chiasm.

classifications.caveats: Defined in cadavers; tumor mass effect changes the apparent position on MRI.

classifications.name: Craniopharyngioma type by infundibulum (Kassam)
classifications.basis: Position of a midline suprasellar craniopharyngioma relative to the infundibulum, which dictates the endonasal corridor (Kassam et al. 2008).

classes.label: Preinfundibular
classes.criterion: Tumor in front of the stalk; stalk displaced posteriorly.
classes.why: Reached through the prechiasmatic / infrachiasmatic window.

classes.label: Transinfundibular
classes.criterion: Tumor within and expanding the stalk.
classes.why: Stalk preservation is often not possible.

classes.label: Retroinfundibular, third ventricle
classes.criterion: Tumor behind the stalk extending up into the third ventricle.
classes.why: Needs a retroinfundibular corridor, sometimes with pituitary transposition.

classes.label: Retroinfundibular, interpeduncular
classes.criterion: Tumor behind the stalk extending down into the interpeduncular cistern.
classes.why: Transdorsum / pituitary transposition approach.

classes.label: Isolated intraventricular
classes.criterion: Tumor confined to the third ventricle without infundibular or suprasellar component.
classes.why: Not suited to an endonasal approach.

classifications.name: Cavernous sinus compartments (endonasal)
classifications.basis: Compartments defined by their relation to the cavernous ICA as seen endonasally (Fernandez-Miranda et al. 2018).

classes.label: Superior
classes.criterion: Above the horizontal cavernous ICA and anterior bend, under the cavernous roof; related to the interclinoid ligament and CN III entering the roof.
classes.why: Knosp 3A extension; CN III at risk.

classes.label: Posterior
classes.criterion: Behind the posterior vertical ICA and posterior bend, between the ICA and the dorsum/clival dura; contains the inferior hypophyseal artery and communicates with the basilar plexus.
classes.why: Reached around the posterior bend; CN VI enters nearby from Dorello's canal.

classes.label: Inferior
classes.criterion: Below the horizontal ICA between the posterior and anterior bends; CN VI and sympathetic fibers cross it toward the lateral compartment.
classes.why: Knosp 3B extension; CN VI at risk.

classes.label: Lateral
classes.criterion: Lateral to the cavernous ICA, containing CN III, IV and V1 in the lateral wall and CN VI.
classes.why: Entered only by working around the ICA; highest cranial nerve risk.

classifications.caveats: Compartment boundaries are defined in the source anatomic study; tumor growth distorts them.

measurements.name: Anterior nasal spine to sphenoid ostium
measurements.what: Straight-line distance from the anterior nasal spine to the natural sphenoid ostium.
measurements.note: Teaching figure ("about 7 cm") used to judge depth with a straight instrument; it varies with facial size, sex and population. Anything deeper than this along the line from the spine toward the ostium (about 30° up from the floor, [[m.sphenoid-ostium-angle]]) is at or beyond the sphenoid face.

measurements.name: Angle from nasal floor to the sphenoid ostium
measurements.what: Angle between the nasal floor and a line from the anterior nasal spine to the sphenoid ostium.
measurements.note: Teaching figure: aiming about 30° up from the floor at roughly 7 cm reaches the ostium; steeper aims go toward the skull base.

measurements.name: Choanal arch to sphenoid ostium
measurements.what: Vertical distance from the upper margin of the choana to the sphenoid ostium in the sphenoethmoidal recess.
measurements.note: Practical rule: the ostium is about 1–1.5 cm above the choanal arch, medial to the superior turbinate. Individual series report wider spreads.

measurements.name: Patency after sphenoid drill-out
measurements.what: Proportion of sphenoid drill-out openings found patent at follow-up in chronic sphenoid sinusitis.
measurements.population: chronic sphenoid sinusitis after failed sphenoidotomy; mean follow-up 17.1 months
measurements.note: One small series, as summarized in a textbook chapter. A separate 9-patient series of mini nasoseptal flaps over bare inferior sphenoid bone (mostly fungal sinusitis) also reported 100% patency at a mean 8.4 months. For comparison, a standard sphenoidotomy for isolated sphenoid disease is reported patent in over 90% at up to 4 years; diffuse chronic sphenoiditis is where it fails.

measurements.name: Sella turcica anteroposterior diameter
measurements.what: Greatest anteroposterior diameter of the sella turcica from tuberculum to dorsum on the midsagittal image.
measurements.note: Normal range from pre-CT lateral radiograph series; CT measurements are comparable. An enlarged or ballooned sella suggests a long-standing intrasellar mass or empty sella.

measurements.name: Sella turcica depth
measurements.what: Depth of the sella from the tuberculum–dorsum line to the deepest point of the floor.
measurements.note: Normal range from pre-CT radiograph series; see [[m.sella-ap-diameter]].

measurements.name: Upper limit of normal pituitary height
measurements.what: Maximum normal craniocaudal height of the pituitary gland on midline coronal/sagittal MRI, by age and physiological state.
measurements.note: Upper limits: about 6 mm in infants and children, 8 mm in men and postmenopausal women, 10 mm in women of reproductive age, 12 mm in late pregnancy and postpartum. A convex upper surface is normal in adolescents and in pregnancy.

measurements.name: Pituitary stalk thickness
measurements.what: Transverse diameter of the pituitary stalk on MRI at the level of the optic chiasm.
measurements.note: About 1.9 mm at its insertion on the gland; the stalk normally tapers from top to bottom. A thick, non-tapering stalk suggests infiltrative disease (hypophysitis, histiocytosis, germinoma, metastasis).

measurements.name: Optic canal length
measurements.what: Length of the optic canal from its intracranial to its orbital opening.
measurements.note: The roof is longer than the floor, so the intracranial opening is oblique; endoscopic decompression opens the medial wall along its full length from the annulus to the tuberculum.

measurements.name: Intraorbital optic nerve length
measurements.what: Length of the optic nerve from the back of the globe to the orbital opening of the optic canal.
measurements.note: Longer than the straight globe-to-apex distance: the slack allows eye movement and some proptosis without stretching the nerve.

measurements.name: Narrowest intercarotid distance
measurements.what: Shortest distance between the medial walls of the two ICAs along their parasellar–supraclinoid course.
measurements.note: Measured between the R and L instances of the landmark. The narrowest point is most often at the supraclinoid/paraclinoid level, less often in the cavernous sinus or the sphenoid; ectatic ICAs in acromegaly narrow it further. This width is the lateral limit of the transtuberculum opening. A narrow sella tends to go with medially placed carotids, so a small sella is a cue to measure this distance before opening.

measurements.name: ICA injury rate in endoscopic endonasal surgery
measurements.what: Proportion of endoscopic endonasal skull base operations complicated by ICA injury.
measurements.population: single high-volume skull base center, all endoscopic endonasal cases
measurements.note: Higher with chondrosarcoma and chordoma, acromegaly and revision or irradiated fields. A national survey of microscopic transsphenoidal surgery reported roughly 1%; survey methods and case mix differ.

measurements.name: CSF leak after vascularized reconstruction of large defects
measurements.what: Postoperative CSF leak rate after endoscopic repair of large dural defects using vascularized flaps.
measurements.note: Compare [[m.csf-leak-free-graft]]; pooled observational series of large dural defects.

measurements.name: CSF leak after free-graft reconstruction of large defects
measurements.what: Postoperative CSF leak rate after endoscopic repair of large dural defects using free grafts only.
measurements.note: The difference from vascularized repair ([[m.csf-leak-vascularized]]) is the basis for routine nasoseptal flap use after high-flow leaks.

measurements.name: CSF leak with lumbar drain in high-risk endonasal defects
measurements.what: Postoperative CSF leak rate with perioperative lumbar drainage after high-risk endoscopic endonasal skull base defects.
measurements.population: randomized trial; high risk = large dural defects in the anterior or posterior cranial fossa or third-ventricle entry
measurements.note: About 21% leaked without a drain in the control arm. The benefit applies to high-risk defects, not routine pituitary surgery. Textbook chapters argue against routine drainage (it adds morbidity) and reserve it for raised intracranial pressure, a persistent high-flow intraoperative leak or a small early postoperative leak; this is consistent with the trial, which tested high-risk defects only. Reported drain use after sphenoid leak repair ranges from 0% to 73% of patients across series.

hazards.name: ICA injury at the sphenoid lateral wall
hazards.site: Parasellar and paraclival carotid prominences in the lateral and posterior sphenoid walls, especially where bone is thin or dehiscent.
hazards.mechanism: Microdebrider, suction, punch or curette on a thin or dehiscent ICA; extending the sphenoidotomy superolaterally; mistaking the carotid prominence for a septum or cell wall; working in the wrong cavity (Onodi cell, contralateral sinus); monopolar current on the wall.
hazards.consequence: Torrential arterial bleeding, hemorrhagic shock, stroke or death; later pseudoaneurysm or carotid–cavernous fistula.
hazards.prevent: Read the axial and coronal CT for dehiscence, septal insertions and ICA course; enlarge the sphenoidotomy inferiorly and medially; no powered instruments or monopolar on the lateral wall; leave mucosa on the prominences; confirm the cavity with navigation.
hazards.recognize: Sudden high-pressure pulsatile bleeding, often a jet that whites out the endoscope, with rapid hemodynamic change.
hazards.rescue: Run the ICA-injury sequence ([[p.ica-injury-management]]): announce it and call for help, second surgeon and two large-bore suctions, keep the endoscope clear of the jet, pack a crushed muscle patch (or close a small tear with bipolar or a clip), keep mean arterial pressure up for collateral flow, then go straight to angiography, and repeat it in the following weeks to catch a delayed pseudoaneurysm ([[h.ica-pseudoaneurysm-delayed]]).

hazards.name: ICA tear from septum avulsion
hazards.site: Posterior insertion of the intersinus or an accessory septum on the carotid prominence.
hazards.mechanism: Grasping, twisting or rocking a septum that inserts on the carotid canal fractures the canal and lacerates the artery.
hazards.consequence: Immediate arterial bleeding, or a partial wall injury that becomes a delayed pseudoaneurysm.
hazards.prevent: Trace every septum to its insertion on axial CT; take septa down with through-cutting instruments or a drill, leaving a stump on the carotid prominence.
hazards.recognize: Pulsatile bleeding at the septal insertion right after septal removal; a bony spicule on the prominence.
hazards.rescue: Do not pull the spicule. Run the ICA-injury sequence ([[p.ica-injury-management]]): announce it and call for help, second surgeon and two large-bore suctions, keep the endoscope clear of the jet, pack a crushed muscle patch (or close a small tear with bipolar or a clip), keep mean arterial pressure up for collateral flow, then go straight to angiography, and repeat it in the following weeks to catch a delayed pseudoaneurysm ([[h.ica-pseudoaneurysm-delayed]]).

hazards.name: Optic nerve injury in the posterior sinuses
hazards.site: Superolateral sphenoid wall (optic prominence, lOCR) or the lateral wall of a sphenoethmoidal (Onodi) cell.
hazards.mechanism: Instrument, microdebrider or suction on a dehiscent canal; heat from drilling without irrigation; monopolar cautery; opening the lateral wall of an Onodi cell mistaken for the sphenoid; compressive packing or orbital apex hematoma.
hazards.consequence: Partial or complete visual loss, often permanent.
hazards.prevent: Identify Onodi cells and canal dehiscence on CT; enter the sphenoid inferomedially; no suction or powered instruments on the optic prominence; bipolar only; diamond burs with irrigation.
hazards.recognize: Intraoperatively exposed sheath or nerve fibers. Postoperatively reduced acuity, color desaturation and a relative afferent pupillary defect — check pupils and vision in recovery.
hazards.rescue: Urgent ophthalmology review; CT for bone fragments or hematoma; remove compressive packing; decompress a compressing fragment or hematoma. Steroids are debated (no clear benefit in the International Optic Nerve Trauma Study).

hazards.name: Cavernous ICA injury during sellar surgery
hazards.site: Parasellar ICA at the lateral limits of the sellar opening, and inside the sella where the ICA indents the gland.
hazards.mechanism: Bone or dural opening too far laterally; sharp curettage against the medial cavernous wall; pulling tumor adherent to the ICA; kissing or ectatic carotids.
hazards.consequence: Arterial hemorrhage, stroke, pseudoaneurysm or carotid–cavernous fistula.
hazards.prevent: Map both ICAs with navigation and micro-Doppler before opening bone and dura laterally; open the dura medially and extend under vision; blunt ring curettes, no blind lateral sweeps; leave invaded medial wall unless a transcavernous resection is planned.
hazards.recognize: Bright pulsatile bleeding from the lateral sella, distinct from dark, welling cavernous venous ooze.
hazards.rescue: Run the ICA-injury sequence ([[p.ica-injury-management]]): announce it and call for help, second surgeon and two large-bore suctions, keep the endoscope clear of the jet, pack a crushed muscle patch (or close a small tear with bipolar or a clip), keep mean arterial pressure up for collateral flow, then go straight to angiography, and repeat it in the following weeks to catch a delayed pseudoaneurysm ([[h.ica-pseudoaneurysm-delayed]]).

hazards.name: Paraclinoid ICA injury
hazards.site: Clinoid and ophthalmic ICA beneath the lOCR and lateral to the mOCR.
hazards.mechanism: Drilling the tuberculum or optic strut too far laterally; dural opening lateral to the mOCR; injury at the distal ring exposing the intradural ICA.
hazards.consequence: Arterial bleeding that may enter the subarachnoid space; stroke.
hazards.prevent: Keep tuberculum bone removal between the mOCRs; Doppler before any dural opening lateral to midline; thin bone to an eggshell and fracture it away rather than drilling on the vessel.
hazards.recognize: Pulsatile bleeding at the superolateral corner of the exposure; blood in the suprasellar cistern.
hazards.rescue: Small tears: bipolar sealing or clip reconstruction. Otherwise run the ICA-injury sequence ([[p.ica-injury-management]]): announce it and call for help, second surgeon and two large-bore suctions, keep the endoscope clear of the jet, pack a crushed muscle patch (or close a small tear with bipolar or a clip), keep mean arterial pressure up for collateral flow, then go straight to angiography, and repeat it in the following weeks to catch a delayed pseudoaneurysm ([[h.ica-pseudoaneurysm-delayed]]).

hazards.name: Petrous ICA injury at the anterior genu
hazards.site: Anterior genu and horizontal petrous ICA at the posterior end of the vidian canal, in the floor of the quadrangular space.
hazards.mechanism: Drilling along the superolateral side of the vidian canal, or past its posterior end without first skeletonizing the ICA; lateralizing the paraclival ICA.
hazards.consequence: Arterial hemorrhage in a deep, narrow corridor that is hard to control.
hazards.prevent: Follow the vidian canal, drilling only its inferior and medial circumference; identify the anterior genu before removing bone behind it; Doppler; diamond burs.
hazards.recognize: Pulsatile bleeding deep in the pterygoid base or medial to V2.
hazards.rescue: Run the ICA-injury sequence ([[p.ica-injury-management]]): announce it and call for help, second surgeon and two large-bore suctions, keep the endoscope clear of the jet, pack a crushed muscle patch (or close a small tear with bipolar or a clip), keep mean arterial pressure up for collateral flow, then go straight to angiography, and repeat it in the following weeks to catch a delayed pseudoaneurysm ([[h.ica-pseudoaneurysm-delayed]]).

hazards.name: Paraclival ICA injury during clival drilling
hazards.site: Paraclival ICAs at the lateral margins of the clival recess.
hazards.mechanism: Drilling beyond the paraclival ICA; tumor (chordoma, chondrosarcoma) thinning or encasing the wall; prior radiation.
hazards.consequence: Arterial hemorrhage, stroke, pseudoaneurysm.
hazards.prevent: Skeletonize both paraclival ICAs early with a diamond bur, leaving an eggshell; Doppler; preoperative CTA and balloon test occlusion when tumor encases the vessel; plan the resection extent around the ICA.
hazards.recognize: Pulsatile bleeding at the lateral clival margin.
hazards.rescue: Run the ICA-injury sequence ([[p.ica-injury-management]]): announce it and call for help, second surgeon and two large-bore suctions, keep the endoscope clear of the jet, pack a crushed muscle patch (or close a small tear with bipolar or a clip), keep mean arterial pressure up for collateral flow, then go straight to angiography, and repeat it in the following weeks to catch a delayed pseudoaneurysm ([[h.ica-pseudoaneurysm-delayed]]).

hazards.name: Parapharyngeal ICA injury
hazards.site: Parapharyngeal ICA posterolateral to the Eustachian tube at the level of the lower clivus and C1.
hazards.mechanism: Nasopharyngeal incisions or dissection lateral to the Eustachian tube; a medialized (retropharyngeal) ICA.
hazards.consequence: Arterial hemorrhage from a vessel without bony cover.
hazards.prevent: Keep nasopharyngeal incisions medial to the torus tubarius and Eustachian tube; read the axial images at C1–C2 for ICA position ([[v.retropharyngeal-ica]]).
hazards.recognize: Pulsatile bleeding lateral in the nasopharynx.
hazards.rescue: Run the ICA-injury sequence ([[p.ica-injury-management]]): announce it and call for help, second surgeon and two large-bore suctions, keep the endoscope clear of the jet, pack a crushed muscle patch (or close a small tear with bipolar or a clip), keep mean arterial pressure up for collateral flow, then go straight to angiography, and repeat it in the following weeks to catch a delayed pseudoaneurysm ([[h.ica-pseudoaneurysm-delayed]]).

hazards.name: Delayed ICA pseudoaneurysm or carotid–cavernous fistula
hazards.site: Any ICA segment that was torn, coagulated or packed, including unrecognized partial wall injuries.
hazards.mechanism: A partial wall injury heals as a pseudoaneurysm, or ruptures into the cavernous sinus as a fistula, days to weeks later.
hazards.consequence: Delayed massive epistaxis; carotid–cavernous fistula (chemosis, proptosis, bruit, ophthalmoplegia); stroke.
hazards.prevent: Angiography after every ICA injury, repeated in the following weeks even if the first is normal; treat any lesion endovascularly before discharge.
hazards.recognize: Sentinel epistaxis or new pulsatile bleeding after leaving theatre; new eye signs.
hazards.rescue: Nasal packing and resuscitation, then emergency endovascular treatment (covered stent, flow diverter, or parent vessel sacrifice after assessing collateral circulation).

hazards.name: Cavernous sinus venous bleeding
hazards.site: Medial cavernous wall, intercavernous connections and the sinus around the ICA.
hazards.mechanism: Opening the medial wall or dura lateral to the sella; tumor removal from within the sinus.
hazards.consequence: Field-flooding venous bleeding; over-packing compresses CN VI and the ICA; air embolism is a rare risk with the head elevated.
hazards.prevent: Head up, controlled normotension, hemostatic matrix loaded before entering the sinus; work one compartment at a time.
hazards.recognize: Dark, non-pulsatile, rapidly welling blood that slows with head-up tilt and gentle pressure.
hazards.rescue: Thrombin-gelatin hemostatic matrix under a cottonoid with patience; bipolar only on dural edges; do not over-pack.

hazards.name: Intercavernous sinus bleeding
hazards.site: Anterior (superior) intercavernous sinus in the upper sellar dura below the tuberculum.
hazards.mechanism: Dural incision through the sinus, or a large sinus covering the whole anterior wall — more likely with a small secreting microadenoma in a normal-sized gland, since a macroadenoma tends to compress the venous channels.
hazards.consequence: Brisk venous bleeding that obscures the dural opening.
hazards.prevent: Open the sellar dura below the sinus; for transtuberculum exposure, coagulate the sinus with bipolar across its width before dividing it.
hazards.recognize: Venous welling from the upper dural edge as it is incised.
hazards.rescue: Bipolar coagulation of the cut dural edges, hemostatic matrix and gentle pressure.

hazards.name: Basilar plexus bleeding
hazards.site: Between the clival bone and the clival dura.
hazards.mechanism: Clival bone removal and dural exposure open the valveless plexus.
hazards.consequence: Heavy blood loss; poor visualization; cautery in the plexus endangers CN VI.
hazards.prevent: Head up; thin the clivus to an eggshell before removing it; have hemostatic matrix ready; open the dura in the midline.
hazards.recognize: Diffuse dark venous bleeding from the exposed clival dura and bone edges.
hazards.rescue: Hemostatic matrix under cottonoids and patience; avoid deep cautery lateral to midline.

hazards.name: Intraoperative CSF leak through the diaphragma
hazards.site: Diaphragma sellae and the arachnoid descending into the sella.
hazards.mechanism: Tearing the thin diaphragm during superior tumor removal; strong suction near the arachnoid; a wide diaphragmatic opening or empty sella.
hazards.consequence: If missed or under-repaired: postoperative CSF rhinorrhea, meningitis, pneumocephalus.
hazards.prevent: Remove the superior tumor last and let the diaphragm descend; low suction near arachnoid; plan reconstruction beforehand (rescue flap incisions).
hazards.recognize: Clear fluid or a visible arachnoid or diaphragmatic hole; Valsalva test before closure; grade it ([[c.csf-leak-grade]]).
hazards.rescue: Graded repair ([[p.skull-base-reconstruction]]): inlay or onlay for a small leak, fat plus buttress for a moderate leak, multilayer with a vascularized flap for high flow.

hazards.name: Postoperative CSF leak after skull base reconstruction
hazards.site: Reconstructed sellar, planum and clival defects; failures cluster at the most dependent edge of the repair (highest CSF pressure) and at its uppermost edge (flap migration or contraction).
hazards.mechanism: Graft or flap failure: flap too small, laid on mucosa, displaced when packing is removed, or lifted by raised CSF pressure. Risk rises with posterior fossa and large anterior fossa defects, ventricular entry, postoperative radiotherapy and obesity (raised intracranial pressure).
hazards.consequence: CSF rhinorrhea, meningitis, tension pneumocephalus.
hazards.prevent: Multilayer repair matched to the defect; vascularized flap on bare bone for high-flow leaks; bolster; lumbar drain for high-risk defects, not routinely ([[m.csf-leak-lumbar-drain]]); avoid straining, nose blowing and early positive-pressure mask ventilation.
hazards.recognize: Clear, salty, positional rhinorrhea; beta-2 transferrin-positive fluid; CT for pneumocephalus; endoscopy for flap position. On postoperative MRI a non-enhancing flap suggests ischemia and may justify re-exploration, but an enhancing flap does not rule out a later leak.
hazards.rescue: Early return to theatre to reposition or augment the repair (preferred for high-flow leaks); lumbar drainage as an adjunct for small leaks; treat meningitis.

hazards.name: Tension pneumocephalus
hazards.site: Intracranial air entering through a skull base defect.
hazards.mechanism: Air drawn in through an incompetent repair (ball-valve), worsened by lumbar drain overdrainage, positive-pressure mask ventilation or nose blowing.
hazards.consequence: Mass effect with falling consciousness.
hazards.prevent: Watertight repair; avoid lumbar drain overdrainage; no early CPAP or bag-mask ventilation.
hazards.recognize: Headache, confusion, falling GCS; CT with frontal lobes compressed and separated by air (Mount Fuji sign).
hazards.rescue: Clamp the lumbar drain, 100% oxygen, head up; urgent repair of the defect; needle or burr hole decompression if life-threatening.

hazards.name: Diabetes insipidus after sellar or suprasellar surgery
hazards.site: Pituitary stalk and posterior lobe.
hazards.mechanism: Manipulation, traction or devascularization of the stalk or posterior lobe.
hazards.consequence: Transient DI is common after sellar surgery; permanent DI is less common and more frequent after craniopharyngioma surgery or stalk sacrifice. A triphasic response (DI, then SIADH, then DI) can occur.
hazards.prevent: Minimize handling of the posterior lobe and stalk; preserve the superior hypophyseal arteries; identify the stalk early in suprasellar dissection.
hazards.recognize: Polyuria with dilute urine and rising serum sodium; watch for delayed hyponatremia about a week after surgery.
hazards.rescue: Fluid balance and desmopressin as needed with serial sodium; endocrinology input; avoid overtreatment.

hazards.name: New hypopituitarism
hazards.site: Normal anterior gland, usually compressed to a rim around the tumor.
hazards.mechanism: Resection or devascularization of normal gland; traction during pituitary transposition.
hazards.consequence: Adrenal insufficiency (potentially fatal), hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, GH deficiency.
hazards.prevent: Locate the normal gland on MRI; extracapsular (pseudocapsule) dissection preserving it; gentle transposition.
hazards.recognize: Postoperative cortisol protocol (a day-1 cortisol when no perioperative steroids were given); hypotension, hyponatremia or fatigue suggest adrenal insufficiency.
hazards.rescue: Stress-dose steroids per protocol and hormone replacement with endocrinology.

hazards.name: Chiasmal ischemia from superior hypophyseal artery loss
hazards.site: Superior hypophyseal branches to the undersurface of the chiasm and optic nerves.
hazards.mechanism: Coagulating or avulsing SHA branches mistaken for tumor feeders; traction on the chiasm.
hazards.consequence: New visual loss despite anatomically intact nerves.
hazards.prevent: Identify the SHAs early at the medial wall of the supraclinoid ICA; sharp extracapsular dissection preserving small vessels on the chiasm and stalk; coagulate only vessels shown to enter tumor.
hazards.recognize: Postoperative visual decline; ischemia on diffusion MRI.
hazards.rescue: No reliable rescue; prevention only. Maintain perfusion and involve ophthalmology.

hazards.name: Optic nerve injury during canal drilling
hazards.site: Optic canal walls, lOCR and medial optic canal at the tuberculum.
hazards.mechanism: Heat from drilling without continuous irrigation; bur skip; bone fragments pushed into the canal; instruments inserted into the canal.
hazards.consequence: Visual loss.
hazards.prevent: Diamond bur with copious irrigation; thin to an eggshell and lift fragments away from the nerve; never insert instruments between bone and nerve.
hazards.recognize: Reduced acuity or a relative afferent pupillary defect after surgery.
hazards.rescue: Urgent ophthalmology; CT for a retained fragment; steroids are debated.

hazards.name: Ophthalmic artery injury
hazards.site: Inferior aspect of the optic nerve within the canal; extradural origin near the optic strut.
hazards.mechanism: Sheath incision in the inferior quadrants; drilling the inferior canal or optic strut near an extradural origin.
hazards.consequence: Orbital hemorrhage; retinal ischemia and blindness.
hazards.prevent: If the sheath is opened, incise it superomedially; identify the artery's origin on CTA.
hazards.recognize: Bleeding from inside the canal or sheath; tense orbit.
hazards.rescue: Gentle pressure and careful bipolar; assess for orbital compartment syndrome and perform lateral canthotomy and cantholysis if present.

hazards.name: ACoA complex and perforator injury
hazards.site: A1–ACoA–A2 complex, recurrent artery of Heubner and hypothalamic perforators above the chiasm.
hazards.mechanism: Dissecting tumor off the ACoA complex; coagulation near perforators; traction.
hazards.consequence: Infarction of hypothalamus, fornix or caudate: memory loss, personality change, hemiparesis.
hazards.prevent: Sharp extracapsular dissection; leave adherent capsule on the complex; identify Heubner along A1.
hazards.recognize: Postoperative cognitive or motor change; infarction on diffusion MRI.
hazards.rescue: Supportive care; prevention is the only protection.

hazards.name: Hypothalamic injury
hazards.site: Floor and walls of the third ventricle.
hazards.mechanism: Stripping adherent craniopharyngioma capsule from the hypothalamus.
hazards.consequence: Hyperphagic obesity, temperature and sleep dysregulation, memory and behavioral change.
hazards.prevent: Grade hypothalamic involvement on MRI and tailor resection; leave adherent capsule; plan adjuvant radiation.
hazards.recognize: Postoperative somnolence, temperature instability and sodium disturbance.
hazards.rescue: Intensive endocrine and metabolic management.

hazards.name: Abducens nerve injury
hazards.site: Dural porus on the midclivus; gulfar segment in Dorello's canal behind the upper paraclival ICA; cavernous segment lateral to the ICA.
hazards.mechanism: Lateral clival dural incisions at the porus; cautery or tight packing in the basilar plexus; tumor dissection at Dorello's canal; work in the inferior or lateral cavernous compartments.
hazards.consequence: Abduction deficit with horizontal diplopia.
hazards.prevent: Open the clival dura in the midline; extend laterally only after locating the porus; EMG stimulation and monitoring; minimal cautery and gentle packing in the plexus.
hazards.recognize: Loss of EMG response intraoperatively; failure of abduction after surgery.
hazards.rescue: Observation — many recover over months; prisms, botulinum toxin or strabismus surgery for persistent palsy.

hazards.name: Basilar perforator and brainstem injury
hazards.site: Basilar trunk and its pontine perforators in the prepontine cistern.
hazards.mechanism: Pulling tumor off the basilar or its perforators; coagulation near the pons.
hazards.consequence: Pontine infarction.
hazards.prevent: Stay in the arachnoid plane; leave adherent tumor; never put traction on perforators.
hazards.recognize: Evoked potential changes; new deficit; infarction on diffusion MRI.
hazards.rescue: No reliable rescue; supportive care.

hazards.name: Cavernous cranial nerve injury (III, IV, V1)
hazards.site: Superior and lateral cavernous compartments and the lateral wall.
hazards.mechanism: Dissection in the superior or lateral compartments; traction on the lateral wall; over-packing.
hazards.consequence: Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia; diplopia; corneal anesthesia.
hazards.prevent: Stay medial to the ICA for adenoma unless the goal justifies lateral work; stimulation mapping; blunt dissection; minimal packing.
hazards.recognize: Postoperative ptosis, pupil change, diplopia or reduced corneal sensation.
hazards.rescue: Observation; eye protection for corneal anesthesia; strabismus or ptosis surgery for persistent deficits.

hazards.name: Trigeminal injury in Meckel's cave
hazards.site: Trigeminal ganglion and V2/V3 roots behind the quadrangular space.
hazards.mechanism: Opening and dissecting within Meckel's cave; traction along V2.
hazards.consequence: Facial numbness or dysesthesia, masticator weakness (V3), neurotrophic keratopathy (V1).
hazards.prevent: Open the quadrangular space dura medially and below the course of CN VI; follow V2 gently; sharp dissection.
hazards.recognize: Postoperative sensory loss in the V1–V3 distributions.
hazards.rescue: Eye protection; neuropathic pain management.

hazards.name: Dry eye after vidian nerve sacrifice
hazards.site: Vidian nerve in its canal at the pterygoid base.
hazards.mechanism: Transection of the vidian nerve to follow its canal to the petrous ICA.
hazards.consequence: Reduced ipsilateral reflex tearing and dry eye.
hazards.prevent: Preserve the nerve when the petrous ICA need not be exposed; when sacrifice is planned, counsel the patient.
hazards.recognize: Dry, gritty eye; reduced Schirmer test.
hazards.rescue: Lubricants, punctal plugs, ophthalmology follow-up.

hazards.name: Loss of the nasoseptal flap pedicle
hazards.site: Posterior septal artery crossing the sphenoid face between the ostium and the choana.
hazards.mechanism: Taking the sphenoidotomy down to the floor, performing the posterior septectomy, or ligating the SPA before the flap is raised.
hazards.consequence: No vascularized septal flap available when a high-flow leak occurs.
hazards.prevent: Decide on reconstruction first: raise the flap, or make rescue-flap incisions that protect the pedicle, before widening the sphenoid inferiorly; keep at least one pedicle intact.
hazards.recognize: Brisk arterial bleeding from the inferior sphenoid face; a pale, non-bleeding flap edge at inset.
hazards.rescue: Use the contralateral nasoseptal flap, a lateral nasal wall (inferior turbinate) flap, or a regional flap: pericranial ([[p.pericranial-flap]]) or temporoparietal fascia ([[p.temporoparietal-fascia-flap]]).

hazards.name: Craniocervical instability
hazards.site: Occipital condyles, C1 anterior arch, dens and its ligaments.
hazards.mechanism: Removal of the C1 arch, dens and transverse/alar ligaments, or extensive condylar resection.
hazards.consequence: Craniocervical instability, pain and progressive neurological deficit.
hazards.prevent: Plan posterior occipitocervical fusion when stabilizers are removed; limit condylar drilling to its medial part; preserve the C1 arch when possible.
hazards.recognize: Neck pain, abnormal motion on dynamic imaging, neurological deterioration.
hazards.rescue: Posterior occipitocervical fusion.

hazards.name: Hypoglossal nerve injury
hazards.site: Hypoglossal canal above the occipital condyle.
hazards.mechanism: Transcondylar drilling into the canal.
hazards.consequence: Ipsilateral tongue weakness; dysphagia and aspiration risk, especially with other lower cranial nerve deficits.
hazards.prevent: Identify the canal on CT; drill only the medial condyle; stop at the cortical bone of the canal.
hazards.recognize: Tongue deviation on protrusion; swallowing difficulty.
hazards.rescue: Swallow assessment and therapy.

hazards.name: Sphenoidotomy stenosis
hazards.site: Margins of the sphenoidotomy.
hazards.mechanism: Small opening; circumferential mucosal stripping with exposed bone; underlying osteitis; a separate transethmoidal opening not joined to the natural ostium (two-hole recirculation).
hazards.consequence: Recurrent sphenoiditis or mucocele.
hazards.prevent: Enlarge the natural ostium inferomedially; preserve mucosa at the margins; join transnasal and transethmoidal openings into one.
hazards.recognize: Recurrent posterior discharge or headache; stenosis at endoscopy; opacified sinus on CT.
hazards.rescue: Revision wide sphenoidotomy or a sphenoid drill-out ([[p.sphenoid-drill-out]]), covering bare bone with a mucosal flap if needed; radical sphenoidectomy ([[p.radical-sphenoidectomy]]) as the last step.

principles.name: Find the sphenoid ostium medial to the superior turbinate
principles.rule: Look for the sphenoid ostium in the sphenoethmoidal recess, medial to the superior turbinate and about 1–1.5 cm above the choanal arch. If it is hidden, remove the inferior third of the superior turbinate — never search higher or more lateral.
principles.why: The natural ostium is the one reproducible, safe door into the sphenoid; above and lateral to it are the skull base, the optic nerve and the posterior ethmoid.
principles.caveat: In a minority of sides the ostium opens lateral to the superior turbinate ([[v.sphenoid-ostium-lateral-to-st]]), and poorly pneumatized sinuses may have a pinhole ostium.

principles.name: Enlarge the sphenoidotomy inferiorly and medially
principles.rule: Widen a sphenoidotomy from the natural ostium downward and toward the septum; the superior and lateral margins are approached last, only under CT and navigation guidance.
principles.why: The optic nerve and ICA sit superolaterally in the sinus; the medial and inferior walls are safe until the posterior septal artery at the lower sphenoid face.
principles.caveat: Taking the opening to the floor sacrifices the posterior septal artery (the nasoseptal flap pedicle) unless the flap has been planned first.

principles.name: Septa lead to the carotid — cut them, never twist them
principles.rule: Trace every sphenoid septum to its posterior insertion on axial CT before surgery, and remove septa with through-cutting instruments or a drill, leaving a stump on the posterior wall.
principles.why: Septa commonly insert on the carotid prominence; twisting one fractures the canal and can tear the ICA.

principles.name: Name every landmark on the sphenoid posterior wall before cutting
principles.rule: Before removing any bone from the posterior wall, name each landmark and confirm it on CT or navigation: sella in the center, planum above, clival recess below, carotid prominences lateral, optic prominences superolateral, lateral opticocarotid recesses between them, medial opticocarotid recesses at the tuberculum corners.
principles.why: The posterior wall is a map of the ICA and optic nerves; once every part is named, the dangerous structures are located before an instrument touches them.
principles.caveat: Conchal and presellar sinuses have no prominences; navigation and Doppler must replace the missing landmarks.

principles.name: The rostrum, not the septum, marks the midline
principles.rule: Define the midline from the vomer–rostrum keel, the symmetric sellar bulge and navigation — not from the intersinus septum.
principles.why: The intersinus septum usually deviates posteriorly and may insert on a carotid prominence; following it leads you off-midline toward the ICA.

principles.name: Binostril, four hands, wide exposure
principles.rule: For sellar and extended work, use both nostrils with a posterior septectomy and two surgeons; open the sphenoid at least from one lateral opticocarotid recess to the other and from the planum to the sphenoid floor.
principles.why: Space lets one surgeon hold a steady, dynamic view while the other works with two instruments — the only setting in which major bleeding can be controlled.
principles.caveat: Small intrasellar lesions may be done through a narrower corridor, but it must be possible to widen it at once.

principles.name: Plan the reconstruction before the sphenoidotomy
principles.rule: Decide the likelihood of a high-flow leak before touching the sphenoid face: harvest the nasoseptal flap first if a leak is expected, or make rescue-flap incisions that protect the pedicle if it is possible.
principles.why: The posterior septal artery crosses the lower sphenoid face; once the face and posterior septum are taken down, the vascularized flap may be gone.

principles.name: The vidian canal leads to the anterior genu
principles.rule: Follow the vidian canal back to the anterior genu of the petrous ICA, drilling only its inferior and medial circumference, before removing bone lateral to the paraclival ICA or around the petrous ICA.
principles.why: The ICA sits at the posterior end of the canal, superolateral to it; drilling the inferomedial side keeps the bur off the vessel until it is exposed.
principles.caveat: The canal may be small, protruding or dehiscent; confirm it on CT and with Doppler.

principles.name: Doppler before every opening near the ICA
principles.rule: Map the ICA with a micro-Doppler probe (and navigation) immediately before opening bone or dura near it: the lateral sellar dura, the tuberculum, the clival dura and the quadrangular space.
principles.why: Tumor displaces the ICA and navigation drifts; the Doppler gives a real-time signal exactly at the instrument tip.

principles.name: Remove sellar tumor inferiorly, then laterally, then superiorly
principles.rule: Debulk the inferior part of a sellar tumor first, then the lateral recesses, and the superior part last; follow the pseudocapsule wherever it exists.
principles.why: Removing the superior part first brings the diaphragma down early, hiding the lateral recesses behind it and making a tear more likely.
principles.caveat: Firm, fibrous tumors do not descend and may need an extended (transtuberculum) approach.

principles.name: Match the repair to the leak
principles.rule: Grade every leak and match the repair: no leak or a small low-flow leak (defect under about 1 cm, little arachnoid opened, no planned radiotherapy) — free graft or fat; high-flow leak (cistern or ventricle opened) or a large defect — multilayer repair with a vascularized flap on bare bone. A lumbar drain is for high-risk defects, not a routine.
principles.why: Vascularized repair halves the leak rate for large defects, and in a randomized trial perioperative lumbar drainage cut it further in high-risk defects ([[m.csf-leak-vascularized]], [[m.csf-leak-lumbar-drain]]). Outside that group routine drainage has no proven benefit and adds its own morbidity, so drains are otherwise kept for raised intracranial pressure or a small early postoperative leak.
principles.caveat: Raised intracranial pressure (obesity, idiopathic intracranial hypertension) defeats good repairs; treat it too. Free grafts are an adjunct to a flap in large defects, not a substitute for one.

principles.name: One flap, two neighboring zones
principles.rule: A single nasoseptal flap can resurface two adjacent skull base zones — frontal, cribriform, planum–sellar, clival — but not three; a defect spanning three needs a second flap or a regional flap.
principles.why: The flap's area is fixed by the septum; stretched over a third zone it is too short to lie flat on bone at every edge. Knowing this before resection decides which pedicles must be protected ([[pr.plan-reconstruction-first]]).
principles.caveat: An expert rule of thumb, not measured coverage: septal size, prior septal surgery and an extended design (onto the nasal floor) change the reach.

principles.name: ICA injury is a rehearsed team drill
principles.rule: Before high-risk cases, brief the team on the ICA-injury plan: who holds the endoscope, where the muscle patch comes from, anesthesia's pressure targets, blood availability and the route to angiography.
principles.why: Outcome is decided in the first minutes; surgeons trained on simulation models control bleeding faster and more reliably.

principles.name: The nasopalatine and naso-axial lines predict the inferior reach
principles.rule: On preoperative sagittal imaging draw the nasopalatine line (rhinion to the posterior hard palate, extended) or the naso-axial line; the lowest point reachable endonasally at the craniovertebral junction is where the line meets the spine.
principles.why: It tells you before surgery whether the dens or C2 target is reachable endonasally or needs a transoral or combined route.
principles.caveat: Both lines are estimates; the naso-axial line was proposed as a more accurate predictor than the nasopalatine line.

principles.name: The ICA segment defines the corridor
principles.rule: Name the ICA segment that bounds your target. Medial to the paraclival and parasellar ICAs is the midline (transsellar, transclival) corridor; lateral to them requires transpterygoid, transcavernous or infrapetrous work with the ICA exposed first.
principles.why: Every coronal-plane endonasal module is defined by its relation to the ICA; crossing a segment before it is exposed is how ICA injuries happen.

procedures.name: Endoscopic transnasal sphenoidotomy
indications: Chronic or recurrent sphenoid sinusitis
Isolated sphenoid disease (fungal ball, mucocele, inverted papilloma biopsy)
First step of transsphenoidal and extended endonasal approaches
Sphenoid CSF leak or encephalocele (with extension)
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, medial to the middle turbinate, through the sphenoethmoidal recess.

preop.check: Pneumatization type and lateral extensions
preop.why: Predicts where the sella and prominences will be ([[c.sphenoid-pneumatization]]).

preop.check: ICA and optic canal: protrusion and dehiscence on bone windows
preop.why: Shows which lateral wall landmarks lack bony cover ([[v.ica-dehiscence]], [[v.optic-canal-dehiscence]]).

preop.check: Posterior insertion of every septum on axial CT
preop.why: Any septum on the carotid prominence is cut, never twisted ([[v.intersinus-septum-on-ica]]).

preop.check: Sphenoethmoidal (Onodi) cell
preop.why: The optic nerve may run in the lateral wall of a cell above the sphenoid ([[v.sphenoethmoidal-cell]]).

preop.check: Ostium position relative to the superior turbinate and choana
preop.why: Plans the transnasal entry ([[m.choana-to-sphenoid-ostium]]).

preop.check: Height of the sphenopalatine foramen on axial and sagittal CT (with navigation)
preop.why: The posterior septal artery leaves the foramen and crosses the sphenoid face at roughly that height, so it predicts how far down the sphenoidotomy can go before the artery, and any future nasoseptal flap pedicle, is at risk ([[s.posterior-septal-artery]]).

steps.do: Optional vasoconstriction of the sphenopalatine territory: a transoral greater palatine canal injection ([[lm.greater-palatine-foramen]], opposite the second molar; needle bent at 45° about 1.5–2 cm from its tip; 1–2 mL of 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine), or a transnasal injection into the lateral wall about 1 cm above the posterior attachment of the middle turbinate.
steps.think: The bend in the needle is the depth stop — the canal ends in the pterygopalatine fossa just below the orbit. Aspirate before injecting.

steps.do: Decongest; gently lateralize the middle turbinate and advance the 0° scope medial to it along the septum to the sphenoethmoidal recess.
steps.think: The choana is my floor marker; the ostium should be 1–1.5 cm above it, medial to the superior turbinate.

steps.do: Identify the natural ostium medial to the superior turbinate; if it is not visible, resect the inferior third of the superior turbinate with through-cutting instruments (some surgeons take up to its lower half, never more).
steps.think: Keep the upper superior turbinate (olfactory mucosa). If I still cannot see it I look lower and more medial, never higher.

steps.do: Confirm the ostium by passing a blunt probe or suction gently into the sinus, and with navigation.
steps.think: The probe goes posteriorly and slightly upward, parallel to the skull base, never laterally.

steps.do: Enlarge the ostium inferiorly and medially with a Kerrison or mushroom punch; stop above the posterior septal artery unless no flap will be needed. If more inferior room is needed but the flap must be kept, first elevate the face mucosa in the subperiosteal plane (a relaxing cut along the vomer helps) and displace it, with the posterior septal artery, downward before removing bone.
steps.think: Will this patient need a nasoseptal flap? If possibly, the inferior face stays or rescue incisions go in now.

steps.do: Inspect the sinus with 0° and 30° scopes; identify optic and carotid prominences, lateral opticocarotid recess, sella and planum; clear disease without stripping the lateral wall.
steps.think: Nothing is pulled off the lateral wall; mucosa over the prominences stays; powered instruments stay medial.

steps.do: Take down the intersinus septum only if needed, cutting or drilling it after rechecking its insertion.
steps.think: Where does this septum end on the axial CT? If on the ICA, drill it and leave a stump.

endpoints: The natural ostium enlarged into one wide opening (joined with any transethmoidal opening)
Disease cleared under direct vision with lateral wall mucosa preserved
Sphenoid roof identified as the reference height for ethmoid work
pitfalls: Entering a posterior ethmoid or Onodi cell and calling it the sphenoid
Two separate openings (natural and transethmoidal) causing mucus recirculation
Enlarging superolaterally toward the optic nerve and ICA
Twisting septa off the carotid prominence
Punching thick, osteitic sphenoid face bone (fungal ball, long-standing sphenoiditis) instead of drilling it
Stripping mucosa from the skull base or medial orbital wall: prolonged edema and new bone formation (neo-osteogenesis) follow
Running a microdebrider inside the sinus rather than at its opening

procedures.name: Transethmoidal sphenoidotomy
indications: Sphenoid disease in a patient undergoing complete ethmoidectomy
Access to the lateral sphenoid wall (optic canal, lateral wall lesions)
procedures.corridor: Through the basal lamella and posterior ethmoid, entering the sphenoid inferomedially and joining the natural ostium.

preop.check: Sphenoethmoidal (Onodi) cell and optic nerve relation
preop.why: The last ethmoid cell may sit above the sphenoid and carry the optic nerve ([[c.delano-optic-nerve]]).

preop.check: Height and slope of the skull base from the planum forward
preop.why: Sets the safe ceiling for the posterior ethmoidectomy.

steps.do: Complete the posterior ethmoidectomy through the basal lamella.
steps.think: The last ethmoid cell is superolateral to the sphenoid; the sphenoid is inferomedial to it.

steps.do: Locate the sphenoid face at the posteroinferior medial corner of the posterior ethmoid, beside the superior turbinate attachment; confirm with navigation or by identifying the natural ostium medial to the superior turbinate. To spare the superior turbinate, use the "Bolger box" — bounded medially by the superior turbinate, inferiorly by its basal lamella, superiorly by the skull base and laterally by the orbital wall — and enter the sphenoid only through the inferomedial half of the box.
steps.think: A horizontal septum with an optic prominence above it means I am in an Onodi cell; the sphenoid is below and medial.

steps.do: Open the sphenoid face inferomedially and join it to the natural ostium, trimming the inferior superior turbinate as needed.
steps.think: One opening, not two.

steps.do: Identify the planum in the sphenoid and use it to clear the ethmoid roof from posterior to anterior.
steps.think: The skull base rises from back to front; working forward from the planum keeps me below it.

endpoints: One wide sphenoidotomy continuous with the posterior ethmoid
Lateral wall landmarks identified; any Onodi cell opened widely
pitfalls: Opening the lateral wall of an Onodi cell (optic nerve)
Entering the sphenoid too high or too lateral
Leaving a bar of bone between the natural and transethmoidal openings

procedures.name: Extended sphenoidotomy (sphenoid drill-out)
indications: Chronic sphenoid sinusitis that recurs after a standard sphenoidotomy (stenosis, osteitis, persistent disease)
The middle step of the escalation for chronic sphenoiditis: standard sphenoidotomy, then drill-out, then radical sphenoidectomy ([[p.radical-sphenoidectomy]])
Targets the usual causes of sphenoidotomy failure: circumferentially denuded bone, too small an opening, and osteitic bone
procedures.corridor: Binostril: both sphenoid faces, the posterior bony septum and the intersinus septum removed to make one common sphenoid opening.

preop.check: Revision anatomy: skull base height and slope, remnant superior turbinate, septal insertions on the carotid prominences, ICA and optic canal dehiscence
preop.why: Previous surgery removes the usual landmarks; the CT and navigation replace them ([[v.intersinus-septum-on-ica]], [[v.ica-dehiscence]]).

preop.check: Osteitis (thick, sclerotic sinus walls) and fungal disease
preop.why: Osteitic bone has to be drilled rather than punched, and bare bone needs mucosal cover to stay open.

preop.check: Septal mucosa and posterior septal artery on each side
preop.why: A small pedicled septal flap may be needed to cover bare bone at the lower rim.

steps.do: Decongest with pledgets medial to the superior turbinates and in the sphenoethmoidal recesses; find each natural ostium or, after previous surgery or when inflammation hides it, the sphenoid floor and roof with navigation.
steps.think: If the superior turbinate is gone I have lost my height marker, and the skull base slopes down toward the back of the sinus — enter low and medial.

steps.do: Widen each sphenoidotomy with rotating punches and Kerrison rongeurs up to the skull base, laterally to the medial orbital wall and down to the sphenoid floor; drill thick bone; keep the microdebrider out of the sinus.
steps.think: Where are the optic and carotid prominences on this side? Nothing is pulled off the lateral wall.

steps.do: Remove the posterior bony septum and rostrum and take the intersinus septum down flush to join both sinuses into one opening.
steps.think: Does the intersinus septum insert on a carotid prominence? Drill it and leave a stump.

steps.do: Cover bare bone at the lower rim with a short (mini) nasoseptal flap — as little as 5–10 mm of posterior septal mucosa on the posterior septal artery.
steps.think: Denuded bone at the rim is what scars the opening shut; mucosa over it keeps it open.

steps.do: At about one week, suction old blood and debris from the sphenoid without disturbing the inferior flap.
steps.think: Around the flap, never under it.

endpoints: One wide common sphenoid opening from skull base to floor and from orbital wall to orbital wall
No circumferential bare bone left at the rim
pitfalls: Drilling too high when the superior turbinate has been removed
Microdebrider engaged inside the sinus rather than at its opening
Denuded or osteitic bone left uncovered at the inferior rim
Twisting septa off a carotid prominence

procedures.name: Radical sphenoidectomy (sphenoid marsupialization)
indications: Chronic sphenoid sinusitis that has failed standard sphenoidotomy and drill-out ([[p.sphenoid-drill-out]]) — the last step of the escalation
A sinus whose mucociliary clearance cannot be relied on: marsupializing it into the nasopharynx makes drainage dependent and blunts the effect of scarring
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, unilateral or bilateral (binostril with a posterior septectomy): the sphenoid floor drilled down flush with the posterior sinus wall so the sinus becomes a recess of the nasopharynx.

preop.check: Floor thickness, vidian canals and pneumatization on CT
preop.why: The floor is drilled down to the level of the posterior wall; the vidian canals mark its lateral edges ([[s.vidian-canal]]).

preop.check: Lateral wall: ICA and optic canal dehiscence, septal insertions
preop.why: The same lateral-wall hazards as any sphenoidotomy.

steps.do: Coagulate and divide the posterior septal artery on the sphenoid face.
steps.think: This gives up the nasoseptal flap on this side — could this patient ever need it?

steps.do: Raise an inferiorly based mucoperiosteal flap from the sphenoid face and rostrum with two vertical incisions running from the edges of the sphenoid opening down to where the sinus ends in the nasopharyngeal roof.
steps.think: This flap will line the new floor; handle it gently.

steps.do: For a bilateral procedure, remove the posterior 1–2 cm of the nasal septum and the intersinus septum to make one wide common opening.
Strip the remaining diseased sphenoid mucosa and drill the sphenoid floor down until it is flush with the posterior sinus wall.
steps.think: No ledge left for mucus to pool behind; the vidian canals are my lateral edges.

steps.do: Lay the flap into the marsupialized cavity over the drilled floor and hold it with packing or tissue glue; remove packs at 3–5 days.
At about one week, suction old blood and debris from the cavity without lifting the inferior flap.

endpoints: Sphenoid floor level with the posterior sinus wall, opening widely and dependently into the nasopharynx
Drilled floor covered by the inferiorly based flap
pitfalls: A residual floor ledge that keeps mucus pooling behind it
Displacing the inferior flap at pack removal or at the first debridement
Drilling the floor lateral to the vidian canal

procedures.name: Endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal transsellar approach
indications: Pituitary adenoma confined to the sella or with suprasellar extension that will descend
Rathke cleft cyst
Pituitary apoplexy decompression
Sellar biopsy
Sellar CSF leak or symptomatic empty sella with leak
procedures.corridor: Binostril: posterior septectomy and wide bilateral sphenoidotomy to the sellar face.

preop.check: MRI: tumor extent, cavernous invasion, position of the normal gland and stalk
preop.why: Decides the extent of resection and where not to curette ([[c.knosp]]).

preop.check: CT or CTA: ICA course, intercarotid distance, kissing or ectatic carotids, dehiscence
preop.why: Sets the safe width of the sellar opening ([[m.intercarotid-distance-narrowest]], [[v.kissing-carotids]]).

preop.check: Sphenoid pneumatization and septal insertions
preop.why: Conchal and presellar sinuses need drilling; septa on the ICA must be cut.

preop.check: Endocrine and visual baseline; perioperative steroid plan
preop.why: Postoperative comparison and prevention of adrenal crisis.

preop.check: Reconstruction plan
preop.why: Suprasellar extension, empty sella or a large diaphragmatic opening raise leak risk: rescue flap or harvested flap.

steps.do: Head up, with modest controlled hypotension (no more than about 20% below baseline). Decongest; lateralize both middle turbinates (partial turbinate resection only if the cavity is narrow); make rescue-flap incisions or raise a full nasoseptal flap on the chosen side. On the other side, cut a small posterior septal mucosal window beside the sphenoid ostium, its lower incision parallel to the ostium, so instruments cross from that nostril while that side's pedicle survives.
steps.think: Leak risk high (suprasellar tumor, empty sella)? Full flap now; otherwise rescue incisions that protect the pedicle.

steps.do: Identify both ostia and enlarge them at first only 1–2 mm upward and outward, pushing the face mucosa and septal artery down with a Freer before bone comes off; detach the posterior bony septum (not forward of the middle turbinate heads) and remove the rostrum; open both sphenoids widely.
steps.think: Width target: lOCR to lOCR, planum to floor. The rostrum defines my midline. Low enough when a straight suction passes into the sinus just below the sellar floor — no inferior ledge of rostrum left.

steps.do: Take down the intersinus and accessory septa flush with the posterior wall using through-cutting instruments or a drill.
steps.think: Septum to the ICA on the axial CT? Drill it and leave a stump.

steps.do: Remove mucosa from the sellar face and read the posterior wall; confirm with navigation.
steps.think: Can I name every bump? The sella is centered between the carotid prominences, not on the septum.

steps.do: Open the sellar floor at its thin central-inferior part and widen it from cavernous sinus to cavernous sinus and from the tuberculum to the floor.
steps.think: Lateral limit: bluish cavernous sinus and the Doppler signal. Upper limit: the intercavernous sinus under the tuberculum.

steps.do: Doppler the dura on both sides; outline the incision with bipolar, then incise the dura medially below the intercavernous sinus and extend it in a cruciate or rectangular pattern.
steps.think: Is the signal where the CT put the ICA? If the carotids are medialized, the dural window shrinks to match.

steps.do: Remove tumor inferiorly, then laterally, then superiorly with ring curettes and suction; use extracapsular (pseudocapsule) dissection where a capsule exists.
steps.think: Where is the normal gland on MRI? Stop at the medial cavernous wall unless it is invaded and resection was planned.

steps.do: Inspect the lateral recesses and suprasellar cavity with 30° and 45° scopes as the diaphragma descends.
steps.think: Residual behind the medial wall or under the diaphragm? Any leak — grade it now.

steps.do: Valsalva test; grade any leak and reconstruct accordingly.
steps.think: Grade 0–1: inlay or onlay. Grade 2: fat plus buttress. Grade 3 or cistern opened: vascularized flap ([[p.skull-base-reconstruction]]).

steps.do: Postoperative endocrine watch: sodium and urine output for diabetes insipidus and SIADH; cortisol on day 1 when no perioperative steroids were given. Withhold saline irrigation for 2–3 weeks, since it can mask CSF rhinorrhea.
steps.think: Clear drip on bending forward or a salty taste is CSF until proven otherwise.

endpoints: Tumor cleared from both lateral recesses and the suprasellar cavity with the normal gland preserved
Diaphragma descended; leak graded and repaired
Hemostasis without packing against the ICA
pitfalls: Opening off-midline by following the septum
Removing the superior part first so the diaphragma collapses early
Lateral curettage against an ICA that indents the gland ([[v.ica-indenting-pituitary]])
No reconstruction plan when the diaphragma tears
Posterior septectomy carried forward of the middle turbinate heads: prolonged septal crusting
An inferior ledge of rostrum or sphenoid floor left behind, blocking instruments to the sella and planum

procedures.name: Endoscopic transplanum–transtuberculum approach
indications: Tuberculum sellae and planum sphenoidale meningioma
Craniopharyngioma (pre-, trans- and retroinfundibular)
Pituitary adenoma with suprasellar extension that will not descend
Rathke cleft cyst with suprasellar extension
procedures.corridor: Binostril: wide sphenoidotomy and bilateral posterior ethmoidectomy to the posterior ethmoidal arteries; bone removal of the tuberculum and posterior planum between the optic canals.

preop.check: MRI: tumor relation to the chiasm, optic canals, A1/ACoA complex, stalk and hypothalamus
preop.why: Selects the corridor and defines stop points ([[c.craniopharyngioma-infundibulum]]).

preop.check: Lateral extension beyond the ICA or over the anterior clinoid; optic canal invasion
preop.why: Tumor lateral to the ICA or optic nerve may be better reached transcranially.

preop.check: Chiasm position
preop.why: A prefixed chiasm narrows the prechiasmatic window ([[c.chiasm-position]]).

preop.check: CTA: supraclinoid ICA, A1/ACoA displacement, narrowest intercarotid distance
preop.why: Defines the lateral bony limits.

preop.check: Nasoseptal flap availability and lumbar drain plan
preop.why: A high-flow leak is certain.

steps.do: Harvest the nasoseptal flap and park it in the nasopharynx or maxillary sinus.
steps.think: This leak will be high-flow: the flap comes first.

steps.do: Wide bilateral sphenoidotomy with posterior septectomy; bilateral posterior ethmoidectomy exposing the planum up to the posterior ethmoidal arteries.
steps.think: Anterior limit: the posterior ethmoidal arteries, to spare olfaction, unless the tumor extends further.

steps.do: Identify both medial and lateral opticocarotid recesses; confirm ICA and optic nerve positions with navigation and Doppler.
steps.think: My lateral bony limit at the tuberculum is the mOCR on each side.

steps.do: Thin the tuberculum, upper sellar face and posterior planum with a diamond bur under irrigation to an eggshell and lift it away; open the medial optic canals if the tumor enters them. Over a meningioma, drill out the thickened, hypervascular bone at its base: this removes much of its blood supply.
steps.think: Heat off the optic nerves; stay between the mOCRs; the intercavernous sinus is right under this bone. Every osteotomy — midline from posterior to anterior, out to both optic canals, joined across the planum — is finished before the dura is opened, so bleeding from drilling never floods the intradural stage.

steps.do: Coagulate the superior intercavernous sinus across its width and divide it; open the planum and sellar dura above and below it and join the openings.
steps.think: Doppler again before cutting dura lateral to midline.

steps.do: Meningioma: coagulate the dural base, debulk internally, then dissect the capsule off the optic apparatus and vessels in the arachnoid plane.
steps.think: Every small vessel on the chiasm is a superior hypophyseal branch until proven otherwise; leave adherent capsule on the ACoA complex.

steps.do: Craniopharyngioma: find the stalk and its relation to the tumor, choose the pre-, trans- or retroinfundibular corridor, open and drain the cyst, debulk, and dissect the capsule only where a plane exists.
steps.think: Stop point: capsule fused to the hypothalamus — leave it and plan radiation.

steps.do: Inspect with angled scopes for residual; achieve hemostasis with warm irrigation and bipolar.
Multilayer closure: intradural inlay graft, extradural onlay, nasoseptal flap on bare bone, bolster; lumbar drain for high-risk defects.
steps.think: Flap on bone all round, no mucosa under it ([[p.skull-base-reconstruction]]).

endpoints: Tumor removed with the optic apparatus, superior hypophyseal arteries, ACoA complex and stalk preserved as planned
Involved optic canals decompressed
Watertight multilayer vascularized repair
pitfalls: Drilling lateral to the mOCR onto the paraclinoid ICA
Coagulating superior hypophyseal arteries as tumor feeders
Pursuing tumor lateral to the optic nerve or ICA endonasally
Flap laid partly on mucosa
Opening dura before the bony exposure is complete
An inferior ledge of rostrum left, blocking instruments to the planum

procedures.name: Endoscopic endonasal transclival approach (upper, middle, lower)
indications: Clival chordoma
Petroclival chondrosarcoma (with lateral modules)
Ventral brainstem and prepontine lesions (meningioma, epidermoid)
Retroinfundibular craniopharyngioma and interpeduncular lesions (upper clivus, with pituitary transposition)
procedures.corridor: Binostril: upper third through the sella with pituitary transposition; middle third through the clival recess between the paraclival ICAs; lower third through the nasopharynx below the sphenoid floor to the foramen magnum.

preop.check: Tumor extent by clival third and relation to the paraclival ICAs, basilar artery and brainstem
preop.why: Chooses the modules ([[c.clivus-thirds]]).

preop.check: CTA and balloon test occlusion when tumor encases the ICA
preop.why: Plans the response if the ICA is injured or must be sacrificed.

preop.check: Lateral extension to the petrous apex, Meckel's cave or hypoglossal canal
preop.why: Adds transpterygoid or far-medial modules.

preop.check: Nasopalatine or naso-axial line
preop.why: Predicts the inferior reach ([[pr.inferior-limit-npl]]).

preop.check: Flap length (extended flap for lower clival defects) and lumbar drain
preop.why: Posterior fossa defects leak most.

steps.do: Position the head slightly flexed, which opens the line of sight to the sphenoid and clivus and lets blood pool away from the field. Harvest an extended nasoseptal flap on the side opposite the tumor's most lateral extension and park it in a widely opened maxillary sinus, clear of the clival corridor; wide bilateral sphenoidotomy with posterior septectomy; flatten the rostrum and sphenoid floor down to the vidian canals.
steps.think: The vidian canals mark the lower paraclival ICAs; the floor between them is the lower edge of my middle-third window.

steps.do: Skeletonize both paraclival ICAs with a diamond bur, leaving eggshell bone; confirm with Doppler.
steps.think: These two lines are my lateral limits for the middle third.

steps.do: Middle third: drill the clival recess between the paraclival ICAs from the sellar floor to the sphenoid floor; control basilar plexus bleeding.
steps.think: Head up, hemostatic matrix ready, stay midline.

steps.do: Upper third when needed: expose the sella, transpose the pituitary (interdural or extradural), dividing the inferior hypophyseal arteries, and remove the dorsum and posterior clinoids.
steps.think: The inferior hypophyseal artery is the only arterial tether: coagulate it away from the ICA wall.

steps.do: Lower third: raise an inferiorly based nasopharyngeal flap of mucosa and pharyngobasilar fascia medial to the Eustachian tubes, detach or resect the longus capitis, drill the lower clivus to the foramen magnum, and extend far-medially through the medial condyle if needed.
steps.think: Lateral limits: the Eustachian tubes (parapharyngeal ICA behind them) and the hypoglossal canal.

steps.do: Resect extradural tumor with the involved bone; open the dura in the midline only for intradural tumor, stimulating for CN VI before any lateral dural cut.
steps.think: Where is the dural porus? Midline first.

steps.do: Intradural dissection in the prepontine cistern along the arachnoid plane, preserving the basilar perforators and CN VI.
steps.think: Tumor stuck to perforators stays.

steps.do: Reconstruct: inlay graft, fat to fill the clival dead space, extended nasoseptal flap on bare bone; lumbar drain for posterior fossa defects.
steps.think: A posterior fossa leak is the highest-risk defect; the flap must reach and lie flat.

endpoints: Tumor and involved bone resected between the ICAs, with planned lateral modules
CN VI function preserved
Vascularized repair covering the whole defect
pitfalls: Lateral clival dural incision through the abducens dural porus
Drilling lateral to the paraclival ICA before exposing it
Flap too short for a lower clival defect
Cautery deep in the basilar plexus near CN VI

procedures.name: Endoscopic transpterygoid approach (medial and lateral extensions)
indications: CSF leak or meningoencephalocele of the sphenoid lateral recess
Infrapetrous access to the petrous apex
Meckel's cave and quadrangular space lesions
Lesions of the pterygoid base and pterygopalatine fossa extending to the skull base
procedures.corridor: Ipsilateral wide maxillary antrostomy or medial maxillectomy, through the posterior maxillary wall into the pterygopalatine fossa, then through the pterygoid base between V2 and the vidian canal.

preop.check: Lateral recess pneumatization and position of V2 and the vidian canal
preop.why: Defines how much pterygoid bone must be drilled ([[v.lateral-recess-pneumatization]]).

preop.check: Petrous ICA and anterior genu
preop.why: Posterior extensions work around it.

preop.check: Side of any planned nasoseptal flap; consent for vidian sacrifice
preop.why: Protect the pedicle; warn of dry eye.

steps.do: Wide maxillary antrostomy or medial maxillectomy; control the sphenopalatine and posterior nasal arteries, preserving the nasoseptal pedicle on the flap side.
steps.think: Which side carries the flap? That pedicle stays.

steps.do: Remove the posterior maxillary wall and bipolar all exposed PPF fat before handling it (it is threaded with small vessels that otherwise ooze throughout); open the PPF periosteum and displace its fat and vessels laterally to expose V2 at the foramen rotundum, the vidian nerve and the pterygoid base.
steps.think: V2 superolateral, vidian inferomedial: the bone between them is the pterygoid wedge.

steps.do: Medial extension: drill the pterygoid base between V2 and the vidian canal to open the lateral recess of the sphenoid.
steps.think: For a lateral recess leak this is enough — stop here and repair, leaving the medial soft-tissue bridge that carries the vidian nerve and the V2 (infraorbital) branches intact.

steps.do: Posterior extension: follow the vidian canal back, drilling its inferior and medial circumference, to the anterior genu; skeletonize the horizontal petrous and lower paraclival ICA.
steps.think: Genu found before any bone lateral or posterior to it comes off.

steps.do: Quadrangular space: open the dura bounded by the paraclival ICA, the petrous ICA, the course of CN VI and V2 to enter Meckel's cave.
steps.think: Stay below the course of CN VI; enter inferiorly and medially.

steps.do: Repair any dural defect with fat or fascia and a vascularized flap; for a lateral recess leak, strip the recess mucosa and fill or line it.
steps.think: Mucosa off the recess walls before the graft goes in.

endpoints: Target reached with V2 and the ICA identified and protected
Any CSF exposure repaired with vascularized tissue
pitfalls: Drilling superolateral to the vidian canal onto the ICA
Confusing V2 with the vidian nerve
Losing the nasoseptal pedicle while ligating the SPA on the flap side

procedures.name: Endoscopic endonasal transcavernous approach
indications: Functioning pituitary adenoma invading the medial cavernous wall or cavernous compartments
Selected non-functioning adenoma in accessible compartments
Biopsy of cavernous sinus lesions
Posterior clinoidectomy for retrosellar access
procedures.corridor: Wide sphenoidotomy (with a transpterygoid step for the lateral compartment), through the medial cavernous wall around the parasellar and paraclival ICA.

preop.check: Knosp grade and which compartments are involved
preop.why: Defines the target and risk ([[c.knosp]], [[c.cavernous-sinus-compartments]]).

preop.check: CTA: ICA course and caliber
preop.why: The ICA is inside the working area.

preop.check: Cranial nerve baseline and the goal (remission versus decompression)
preop.why: Justifies — or not — the nerve risk of each compartment.

steps.do: Wide bilateral sphenoidotomy; expose the sella and the parasellar and paraclival carotid prominences on the involved side; add a transpterygoid step for lateral access.
steps.think: Which compartment is involved on MRI: superior, posterior, inferior or lateral?

steps.do: Remove bone over the sella and parasellar ICA; map the ICA with Doppler.
Resect the sellar component; open the medial cavernous wall and cut its parasellar ligaments to mobilize or resect it.
steps.think: Hemostatic matrix loaded, head up, one compartment at a time.

steps.do: Enter the involved compartment: superior (above the horizontal ICA), posterior (behind the posterior bend, with the inferior hypophyseal artery), or inferior (below the horizontal ICA, with CN VI crossing).
steps.think: Does removing this piece change the outcome (remission) enough to justify the nerve risk?
