steps.do: Lateral compartment only for strong indications, with ICA control and cranial nerve stimulation.
For retrosellar access, remove the posterior clinoid through the superior and posterior compartments; then hemostasis and reconstruction.

endpoints: Invaded medial wall and involved compartments cleared as planned
ICA intact; cranial nerve function preserved
pitfalls: Entering the lateral compartment without a strong indication
Over-packing the sinus around CN VI
Tearing meningohypophyseal branches at the ICA wall

procedures.name: Endoscopic medial petrous apex approach
indications: Cholesterol granuloma or mucocele of the petrous apex abutting the sphenoid or clival recess
Petrous apicitis needing drainage
Biopsy of medial petrous apex lesions
procedures.corridor: Wide sphenoidotomy; a medial route through the clival recess medial to the paraclival ICA when the lesion expands medially, or an infrapetrous (transpterygoid) route below the petrous ICA when it does not.

preop.check: Does the lesion abut the posterior sphenoid wall medial to the paraclival ICA?
preop.why: If so, the medial route needs no ICA mobilization.

preop.check: MRI signal (T1 and T2 bright, non-enhancing = cholesterol granuloma)
preop.why: The goal is drainage, not resection.

preop.check: ICA course and dehiscence next to the lesion
preop.why: The lesion wall often lies directly on the ICA.

steps.do: Wide sphenoidotomy (bilateral with posterior septectomy for instrument angle); raise a flap if it will line the drainage tract.
steps.think: A vascularized lining keeps the opening patent.

steps.do: Identify the paraclival ICA and the bulge of the lesion in the clival recess medial and posterior to it; confirm with navigation and Doppler.
steps.think: Is the lesion truly medial to the ICA here? If not, switch to the infrapetrous route.

steps.do: Drill into the lesion medial to the ICA and open it widely; drain and irrigate.
steps.think: The lateral cyst wall lies on the ICA and CN VI: no curettage there.

steps.do: Infrapetrous route if needed: follow the vidian canal to the anterior genu and drill below the horizontal petrous ICA into the apex.
Marsupialize: line the opening with a vascularized flap or place a stent to reduce restenosis.

endpoints: Wide, lined communication between the lesion and the sphenoid
ICA and CN VI undisturbed
pitfalls: Choosing the medial route when the lesion does not reach the sphenoid
Curetting the cyst wall against the ICA
Restenosis of an unlined opening

procedures.name: Endoscopic optic nerve decompression
indications: Compressive optic neuropathy from fibro-osseous lesions, mucocele or tumor at the optic canal
Selected traumatic optic neuropathy (controversial; no proven benefit over observation or steroids in the International Optic Nerve Trauma Study)
Part of orbital apex decompression
procedures.corridor: Complete sphenoethmoidectomy on the involved side; the medial optic canal wall from the orbital apex to the tuberculum.

preop.check: Optic nerve relation to the sphenoid and any Onodi cell
preop.why: The canal may lie in an Onodi cell ([[c.delano-optic-nerve]]).

preop.check: Fractures or fragments in the canal
preop.why: Plans fragment removal.

preop.check: ICA dehiscence and ophthalmic artery origin
preop.why: The optic strut drilling field includes the clinoid ICA and occasionally the ophthalmic origin ([[v.ophthalmic-artery-extradural-origin]]).

preop.check: Full ophthalmologic baseline: acuity, color vision, fields, pupils, proptosis, intraocular pressure and fundus; visual evoked potentials in an unconscious patient; ultrasound if a hematoma is suspected
preop.why: Indication and outcome, and a treatable orbital cause is not missed.

preop.check: Contraindications: complete disruption of the nerve or chiasm, complete optic atrophy, carotid–cavernous fistula, or unfitness for general anesthesia
preop.why: Opening the canal cannot help a transected or atrophic nerve, and visual loss from a fistula needs the fistula treated.

preop.check: Medical treatment of the cause
preop.why: Steroids for traumatic optic neuropathy are contested ([[dz.traumatic-optic-neuropathy]]: no benefit shown in the International Optic Nerve Trauma Study, and high-dose steroids raised mortality after head injury in CRASH); thyroid eye disease may respond to radiotherapy, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension to diuretics.

steps.do: Complete posterior ethmoidectomy and wide sphenoidotomy (resecting or swinging the middle turbinate if the corridor is narrow); identify the posterior lamina papyracea, optic prominence and lateral opticocarotid recess.
steps.think: Is the canal in the sphenoid or in an Onodi cell? The posterior septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery crosses the lower edge of the sphenoidotomy — coagulate it if it bleeds.

steps.do: In the posterior ethmoid about 1 cm in front of the sphenoid face, fracture the lamina papyracea and flake it back toward the optic strut, leaving periorbita intact; where the bone becomes too thick for hand instruments (orbital apex, medial canal wall), thin it with a diamond bur under constant irrigation, or an ultrasonic bone aspirator.
steps.think: Irrigate continuously; thin to an eggshell only.

steps.do: Lift the thinned bone away from the nerve from the annulus back to the tuberculum, opening the medial half of the canal circumference; drill the lateral opticocarotid recess (optic strut) for inferior decompression when needed.
steps.think: The clinoid ICA lies behind the strut.

steps.do: Optional sheath incision (debated): superomedially, including the annulus, away from the ophthalmic artery below.
steps.think: Does the evidence justify opening the sheath in this patient? Carried through the annulus, the cut can injure the rectus origins (diplopia). If CSF escapes, seal it with fibrin glue or a small free mucosal graft and minimal absorbable packing — nothing that presses on the nerve.

steps.do: Hemostasis without packing on the nerve.
Postoperatively: no nasal packing; a carefully tapered high-dose steroid course, adjusted to serial eye examinations.
steps.think: Vision worse than before surgery: urgent examination and CT for a hematoma or retained fragment.

endpoints: Medial canal wall removed from the annulus to the tuberculum — about 180° of the canal circumference
Nerve sheath inspected for hematoma
No packing against the nerve
pitfalls: Decompressing the wall of an Onodi cell believed to be sphenoid
Heat injury from drilling
Inferior sheath incision onto the ophthalmic artery
Sheath incision carried across the annulus onto the rectus origins (diplopia)
Packing a sheath CSF leak against the nerve

procedures.name: Endoscopic endonasal transodontoid approach
indications: Basilar invagination with ventral cervicomedullary compression
Rheumatoid or inflammatory pannus at C1–C2
Odontoid lesions compressing the cervicomedullary junction
procedures.corridor: Binostril, below the sphenoid floor, through the nasopharynx to the lower clivus, C1 anterior arch and dens, limited inferiorly by the nasopalatine or naso-axial line.

preop.check: Nasopalatine or naso-axial line on sagittal CT
preop.why: Confirms the dens is reachable ([[pr.inferior-limit-npl]]).

preop.check: Parapharyngeal ICA position at C1–C2
preop.why: Keeps incisions medial ([[v.retropharyngeal-ica]]).

preop.check: Stability and fusion plan
preop.why: Removing the C1 arch and dens usually requires posterior fusion.

steps.do: Limited posterior septectomy; raise an inferiorly based U-shaped nasopharyngeal flap of mucosa and pharyngobasilar fascia medial to the Eustachian tubes.
steps.think: The Eustachian tubes are my lateral limits.

steps.do: Detach the longus capitis and colli from the lower clivus and C1 in the midline; identify the anterior arch of C1 and the basion.
steps.think: Confirm midline with navigation before any drilling.

steps.do: Remove the middle of the C1 anterior arch, or preserve it if the dens can be reached above it.
Core out the dens from the tip downward with a drill, then remove the thin cortical shell; divide the apical and alar ligaments.
steps.think: Hollow first, shell last, lifting the shell away from the dura.

steps.do: Remove pannus down to the tectorial membrane, preserving it to avoid a CSF leak; confirm decompression on imaging or navigation.
steps.think: Is the ventral cervicomedullary junction now free?

steps.do: Close the nasopharyngeal flap; proceed to posterior occipitocervical fusion as planned.

endpoints: Dens and pannus removed with the tectorial membrane intact
Stability restored by planned fusion
pitfalls: Incising lateral to the Eustachian tube
Target below the reach of the nasal corridor
Breaching the tectorial membrane and dura

procedures.name: Endoscopic skull base reconstruction (multilayer, gasket seal, nasoseptal flap inset)
indications: Planned dural defects after sellar and extended endonasal approaches
Intraoperative CSF leak
Sphenoid CSF leak and encephalocele repair (see also [[p.csf-leak-repair]])
procedures.corridor: The surgical defect; flap from the nasal septum.

preop.check: Expected defect size and flow
preop.why: A high-flow leak (cistern or ventricle) needs a vascularized repair ([[pr.reconstruction-matches-leak]]).

preop.check: Flap availability: prior septal surgery, perforation, pedicle side
preop.why: Plan an alternative flap if the nasoseptal flap is unavailable.

preop.check: Risk factors for failure: obesity or raised intracranial pressure, postoperative radiotherapy, ventricular entry, large anterior or posterior fossa defects
preop.why: Adds layers and, for high-risk defects, a lumbar drain.

preop.check: Defect map: suprachiasmatic (anterior fossa) or infrachiasmatic (sella, clivus) in the sagittal plane; extension lateral to the pterygoid plates in the coronal plane
preop.why: Lateral extension usually means sacrificing the ipsilateral internal maxillary artery, and with it every flap that depends on it on that side.

preop.check: Flap reach and area against the defect
preop.why: A well-designed nasoseptal flap (up to about 25 cm²) reaches from the posterior table of the frontal sinus to the sella and from one lamina papyracea to the other, or covers a full clivectomy — but spans only two neighboring zones ([[pr.one-flap-two-regions]]). Local alternatives are small: inferior turbinate flap about 2.4 cm²; middle turbinate flap about 5.6 cm², reaching the sella only if the turbinate is at least about 4 cm long (a concha bullosa makes harvest harder); hard palate flap about 15 cm², with a risk of oroantral fistula. Regional flaps: pericranial ([[p.pericranial-flap]], about 29–35 cm²), temporoparietal fascia ([[p.temporoparietal-fascia-flap]], about 238 cm²) and facial buccinator (about 19 cm², with a risk of epiphora).

preop.check: Age under about 14 years
preop.why: The face is small relative to the skull, so a nasoseptal flap may be too short to reach the defect; plan an alternative.

steps.do: Grade the leak and measure the defect; strip all mucosa from the bone around its margins.
steps.think: The flap must lie on bare bone all round.

steps.do: Fill dead space where needed (sellar cavity, clival defect) with autologous fat, without over-packing under the chiasm.
steps.think: Fat supports the repair, but too much in the sella compresses the chiasm.

steps.do: Inlay: place collagen matrix or fascia intradurally, oversized well beyond the dural edges to allow for overlap and shrinkage; where the falx blocks an anterior defect, split the front of the graft into two "trouser legs" that straddle it.
Gasket seal where the bony edges allow: fascia lata over the defect with a rigid buttress (bone, cartilage or an absorbable plate) countersunk into the bony opening.
steps.think: Only possible when the bony rim will hold the buttress. Autologous bone and cartilage tend to resorb, so their job is early support.

steps.do: Onlay: rotate the nasoseptal flap on its posterior septal pedicle to cover the defect with generous overlap onto bone, without twisting or stretching the pedicle.
steps.think: Pedicle along the sphenoid floor; edges flat, no folds, periosteal side down.

steps.do: Secure with absorbable packing held by a nasal balloon (sealant is optional over a well-placed multilayer flap repair); lumbar drain for high-risk defects, not routinely.
steps.think: The balloon holds the packing, not the flap: inflate only enough to steady the packing — over-inflation can push the graft intracranially, compress the pedicle or press on the chiasm.

steps.do: Postoperative precautions: head up, no nose blowing or straining, no early positive-pressure mask ventilation, stool softeners. The balloon usually stays 2–5 days (packing 4–7 days after a sphenoid leak repair); no saline irrigation for the first 2–3 weeks, since it can mask CSF rhinorrhea. Antibiotic cover while packing is in place is common but regimens vary; its aim is the sinonasal infection that follows this surgery, not meningitis prevention.

endpoints: All planned layers in place without gaps
Flap on bone covering the whole defect
No leak on Valsalva
pitfalls: Flap laid on residual mucosa (failure, mucocele)
Flap too small or pedicle twisted
Over-packing the sella under the chiasm
Balloon inflated to "hold" the flap: it can displace the graft intracranially, compress the pedicle or press on the chiasm
Free grafts alone for a large or high-flow defect

procedures.name: Pericranial flap for endonasal skull base reconstruction
indications: Large anterior skull base defect when the nasoseptal flap is unavailable (prior septal surgery, tumor involvement, lost pedicle) or too small
Rescue after loss of both nasoseptal pedicles ([[h.nsf-pedicle-injury]])
procedures.corridor: From the forehead, pedicled on the supraorbital and supratrochlear vessels, through a bony window at the nasion and a Draf III frontal opening into the nasal cavity.

preop.check: Supraorbital and supratrochlear vessels intact (no previous coronal or forehead surgery that divided them)
preop.why: They are the flap's only supply.

preop.check: Frontal sinus anatomy for a Draf III
preop.why: The flap reaches the nose through a modified endoscopic Lothrop opening ([[p.draf-iii]]).

steps.do: Make a bicoronal scalp incision and raise the scalp in the subgaleal plane, leaving the pericranium on the skull.
steps.think: The pericranium is the flap: do not thin or perforate it.

steps.do: Incise the pericranium far back and elevate it forward to the supraorbital rims, preserving the supraorbital and supratrochlear vessels as its pedicle.
steps.think: The pedicle is at the rims; that is where elevation needs the most care.

steps.do: Endoscopically, perform a modified Lothrop (Draf III) to open a wide transport corridor from the frontal sinus into the nose.
Open a small bony window through the nasion into the frontal sinus and pass the flap through it and the Draf III opening onto the defect.
steps.think: Is the window wide enough that the pedicle is not strangled?

steps.do: Inset the flap over the whole defect on denuded bone without kinking the pedicle at the nasion.

endpoints: Flap covering the defect with bone contact all round
Pedicle unkinked through the nasion window
pitfalls: Dividing the supraorbital or supratrochlear vessels during elevation
A nasion window or frontal opening too narrow for the flap bulk
Transposing without a Draf III corridor

procedures.name: Temporoparietal fascia flap with transpterygoid transfer
indications: Large clival, sellar or parasellar defects when endonasal flaps are unavailable or too small
procedures.corridor: From the temple, pedicled on the superficial temporal vessels, through a tunnel from the temporal fossa deep to the zygomatic arch into the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae, then through a transpterygoid opening into the nasal cavity.

preop.check: Superficial temporal artery signal; no previous temporal or coronal surgery on that side
preop.why: It is the flap's only supply.

preop.check: Side of the transfer route
preop.why: The route sacrifices the sphenopalatine and posterior nasal arteries on that side, and with them that side's nasoseptal flap.

steps.do: Endoscopically, ligate the sphenopalatine and posterior nasal arteries, remove the posterior maxillary wall and open the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae; enlarge the route by removing the anterior part of the pterygoid process.
Through a hemicoronal incision, harvest the temporoparietal fascia on the superficial temporal vessels.
steps.think: Keep the anterior dissection limited: the frontal branch of the facial nerve runs with this fascia there.

steps.do: Develop a tunnel from the temporal fossa deep to the zygomatic arch into the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae, dilate it (a tube or sheath can bridge it) and draw the flap through into the nose.
steps.think: A tight tunnel strangles the pedicle; make it generous.

steps.do: Inset the fascia over the defect on denuded bone without twisting the pedicle.

endpoints: Perfused fascia covering the defect on bare bone
Pedicle untwisted through the tunnel
pitfalls: Injury to the frontal branch of the facial nerve during harvest (brow paralysis)
Tunnel too narrow, compressing the pedicle
Uncontrolled internal maxillary bleeding while opening the infratemporal route

procedures.name: Management of intraoperative ICA injury
indications: Intraoperative ICA injury during any endonasal procedure

preop.check: For high-risk cases: muscle donor site prepared, blood cross-matched, angiography available, team briefed
preop.why: The first minutes decide the outcome ([[pr.ica-injury-rehearsed]]).

preop.check: Balloon test occlusion or collateral assessment when tumor encases the ICA
preop.why: Knowing whether sacrifice is tolerated changes the options.

steps.do: Recognize and announce: stop, call the senior surgeon, anesthesia and interventional radiology; keep the endoscope in the nose.
steps.think: Stay calm; the endoscope is now the most important instrument.

steps.do: Two surgeons, four hands: one holds the endoscope near the bleeding with the tip out of the jet; the other uses two large-bore suctions — one placed to draw the jet away from the endoscope tip, one at the site — to find the tear.
steps.think: Can I see the hole? Without a view there is no targeted control.

steps.do: Anesthesia keeps normotension or mild hypertension for cerebral perfusion and resuscitates with volume and blood; ipsilateral cervical carotid compression may reduce flow while the site is controlled.
steps.think: Do not let the pressure fall: collateral flow is keeping the brain alive.

steps.do: Control: close a small tear with bipolar or an aneurysm clip; otherwise place a crushed muscle patch (temporalis or thigh) over the tear and hold gentle pressure; packing is the last resort because it can occlude the ICA; if nothing else stops the bleeding, pack to control it and let angiography assess collateral flow.
steps.think: A muscle patch keeps the lumen open; aggressive packing can occlude the ICA or push material intradurally if the dura is open.

steps.do: Once controlled, pack the field over the patch and transfer directly to angiography.
steps.think: No stop on the ward: an unimaged ICA injury is an unfinished operation.

steps.do: Angiography: assess extravasation, pseudoaneurysm, occlusion and collateral flow; treat with a covered stent or flow diverter, or sacrifice the parent vessel if collateral circulation is adequate.
Follow-up: repeat angiography in the following weeks; watch for delayed epistaxis, carotid–cavernous fistula and stroke.

endpoints: Bleeding controlled with the patient hemodynamically stable
Angiographic assessment and definitive endovascular treatment
Repeat angiography planned
pitfalls: Deliberate hypotension worsening cerebral ischemia
Losing the view by withdrawing the endoscope to clean it
Leaving theatre without an angiogram
Over-packing and occluding the ICA

stations.name: Sphenoethmoidal recess, 0°
stations.where: Scope tip medial to the middle turbinate at its posterior end, above the choana, looking posteriorly and slightly up at the sphenoid face.
stations.purpose: Find the natural sphenoid ostium medial to the superior turbinate and judge its height above the choana.

stations.name: Sphenoid posterior wall, 0°
stations.where: Scope tip at the posterior septectomy in the midline of the opened sphenoid, looking straight back at the posterior wall.
stations.purpose: Read the "face" of the sphenoid: name the sella, planum, clival recess, carotid and optic prominences and both opticocarotid recesses before removing bone.

stations.name: Sphenoid lateral recess, 45° from the opposite nostril
stations.where: Scope through the contralateral nostril across the posterior septectomy, tip at the midline of the sphenoid, angled laterally into the lateral recess of the target side.
stations.purpose: Inspect the lateral recess for leak sites and see V2 and the vidian canal without a transpterygoid approach.

stations.name: Optic canal and lateral sphenoid wall, 0°
stations.where: Scope tip in the ipsilateral posterior ethmoid–sphenoid junction, looking posterolaterally at the orbital apex and the superolateral sphenoid wall.
stations.purpose: Follow the optic canal from the orbital apex to the tuberculum and locate the lOCR for decompression or to avoid it.

stations.name: Inside the opened sella, 30°
stations.where: Scope tip at the sellar opening, 30° lens rotated to each side and upward in turn, looking into the lateral recesses of the sella and up toward the diaphragma.
stations.purpose: Check for residual tumor along the medial cavernous walls and under the diaphragma, and inspect for a leak.

stations.name: Suprasellar cistern via transtuberculum, 0°
stations.where: Scope tip at the tuberculum defect, looking up and back into the suprasellar cistern.
stations.purpose: See the optic apparatus, its superior hypophyseal supply, the stalk and the ACoA complex that bound suprasellar dissection.

stations.name: Prepontine cistern via transclival, 0°
stations.where: Scope tip at the level of the sphenoid floor in the clival opening, looking posteriorly through the opened clival dura.
stations.purpose: Show the basilar trunk, its perforators and CN VI that limit transclival resection.

stations.name: Medial petrous apex, 45°
stations.where: Scope through the contralateral nostril across the posterior septectomy, tip at the clival recess, angled posterolaterally behind the paraclival ICA of the target side.
stations.purpose: Judge whether a petrous apex lesion can be drained medial to the paraclival ICA.

stations.name: Pterygoid base and quadrangular space, 0°
stations.where: Scope through the ipsilateral transmaxillary–transpterygoid corridor, tip at the posterior maxillary wall, looking posteriorly at the pterygoid base.
stations.purpose: Relate V2, the vidian canal and the petrous and paraclival ICA to define the quadrangular space before entering Meckel's cave.

stations.name: Lower clivus and craniovertebral junction, 0°
stations.where: Scope tip in the nasopharynx after posterior septectomy, looking posteroinferiorly along the naso-axial line at the lower clivus and C1.
stations.purpose: Define the lateral limits (Eustachian tubes) and the targets (basion, C1 arch, dens) of lower clival and transodontoid work.

stations.name: Parasellar ICA and cavernous sinus, 30°
stations.where: Scope tip at the lateral edge of the sellar opening, 30° lens turned laterally toward the parasellar carotid prominence of the target side.
stations.purpose: Orient to the cavernous compartments around the parasellar ICA before transcavernous work.

stations.name: Central skull base, midsagittal overview
stations.where: Overview camera outside the head, viewing a midsagittal cutaway from the left.
stations.purpose: See the whole midline sequence from planum to dens and how the sphenoid sits between the nose, the sella and the brainstem.

pathways.name: Sphenoid sinus mucociliary clearance
pathways.note: Cilia sweep mucus up the walls toward the ostium high on the anterior wall — against gravity — which is why an obstructed ostium causes stasis and why the sphenoidotomy is enlarged downward.

pathways.name: Sphenoethmoidal recess drainage to the nasopharynx
pathways.note: Posterior-group secretions pass posterosuperior to the torus tubarius into the nasopharynx; anterior-group secretions pass anteroinferior to it.

pathways.name: Pituitary venous drainage
pathways.note: Hypophyseal veins and the intercavernous sinuses drain to the cavernous sinuses and on through the inferior petrosal sinuses to the jugular bulbs; bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling uses this route to lateralize ACTH secretion.
